docs.title: mxlpy
docs.text: mxlpy is a Python package designed to enable mechanistic learning, bridging the gap between mechanistic modeling and machine learning. The package enables you to integrate ordinary differential equation (ODE) models with data-driven techniques. This combination allows for more accurate and interpretable predictions in systems where both physical laws and data-driven insights are valuable. mxlpy thus facilitates the development of models that are not only data-efficient but also robust and capable of capturing complex system dynamics. Choose one of the notebooks below to start your journey!

docs.title: Building and simulating models
docs.text:
In this first notebook you will learn how to build ODE models and do basic simulations with them. This will allow you to create time courses and do steady-state analysis as shown below.

Start learning

docs.title: Other model builders
docs.text:
Not every model is best described as a reaction network. Next to the reaction-based Model, mxlpy offers an OdeModelBuilder for models written directly as differential equations, and a SteadyStateModelBuilder for purely algebraic models, which are evaluated instead of simulated. Both can be scanned and fitted just like a Model.

ODE models Steady-state models

docs.title: Parameter scans
docs.text:
Parameter scans allow you to systematically assess the behaviour of your model dependent on the value of one or more parameters. mxlpy has rountines to scan over, and easily visualise time courses, protocol time courses, and steady states for one or more parameters.

Start learning

docs.title: Metabolic control analysis
docs.text:
Metabolic control analysis answers the question: what happens to the concentrations and fluxes if I slightly perturb the system? It is thus a local measurement about which reactions hold the most control. If you ever read about rate-limiting steps, then this is for you!

Start learning

docs.title: Fitting
docs.text:
Almost every model at some point needs to be fitted to experimental data to be validated. mxlpy offers highly customisable routines for fitting either time series or steady-states.

Start learning

docs.title: Monte Carlo methods
docs.text:
Almost every parameter in biology is better described with a distribution than a single value. Monte-carlo methods allow you to capture the range of possible behaviour your model can exhibit. This is especially useful when you want to understand the uncertainty in your model's predictions. mxlpy offers these Monte Carlo methods for all scans ...

docs.title: Label models
docs.text:
Labelled models allow explicitly mapping the transitions between isotopomers variables.

docs.title: Mechanistic Learning
docs.text:
Mechanistic learning is the intersection of mechanistic modelling and machine learning. mxlpy currently supports two such approaches: hybrid models and neural posterior estimation.

Hybrid models like universal differential equations (UDEs) combine ordinary differential equations based models with neural differential equations (NDEs).

Start learning

Surrogate models replace whole parts of a mechanistic model (or even the entire model) with machine learning models.

This allows combining together multiple models of arbitrary size, without having to worry about the internal state of each model. They are especially useful for improving the description of boundary effects, e.g. a dynamic description of downstream consumption.

Start learning

Neural posterior estimation answers the question: what parameters could have generated the data I measured? Here you use an ODE model and prior knowledge about the parameters of interest to create synthetic data. You then use the generated synthetic data as the features and the input parameters as the targets to train an inverse problem. Once that training is successful, the neural network can now predict the input parameters for real world data.

Start learning

docs.title: Parameterisation
docs.text:
Obtaining experimentally measured parameters can be challenging. Using the Brenda enzymes database we can obtain distributions of enzymatic parameters for a wide range of organisms. These distributions can in turn be used with our Monte-Carlo methods to capture the range of possible behaviour your model can exhibit.

adjoint_sensitivities.time_course returns an AdjointSensitivities object with

  • gradient: the derivative of sum(cotangents * y) with respect to every name in wrt (parameters, and variables for their initial values)
  • simulated: the simulated values at the cotangents' time points and columns
  • method: "adjoint", "forward" or "finite_difference"
  • adjoint: the adjoint state \(\lambda(t)\); \(\lambda(0)\) is the gradient with respect to the initial values

def layer(  # noqa: PLR0917
    x0: float,
    x1: float,
    x2: float,
    x3: float,
    x4: float,
    x5: float,
    w0: float,
    w1: float,
    w2: float,
    w3: float,
    w4: float,
    w5: float,
    b: float,
) -> float:
    return math.tanh(w0 * x0 + w1 * x1 + w2 * x2 + w3 * x3 + w4 * x4 + w5 * x5 + b)


def scaled(h: float, v: float) -> float:
    return v * h


def hybrid(n: int, n_hidden: int) -> Model:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    xs = [f"x{i}" for i in range(n)]
    model = Model().add_variables({x: 1.0 / (i + 1) for i, x in enumerate(xs)})
    for i, x in enumerate(xs):
        model.add_parameter(f"k{i}", 1.0 / (i + 1))
        stoichiometry = {x: -1} | ({xs[i + 1]: 1} if i + 1 < n else {})
        model.add_reaction(
            f"v{i}", fns.mass_action_1s, args=[x, f"k{i}"], stoichiometry=stoichiometry
        )
    for j in range(n_hidden):
        weights = {f"w{j}_{i}": float(rng.normal(0, 0.3)) for i in range(n)}
        model.add_parameters(weights | {f"b{j}": 0.0})
        model.add_derived(f"h{j}", layer, args=[*xs, *weights, f"b{j}"])
        for k, x in enumerate(xs):
            model.add_parameter(f"c{j}_{k}", float(rng.normal(0, 0.05)))
            model.add_reaction(
                f"r{j}_{k}", scaled, args=[f"h{j}", f"c{j}_{k}"], stoichiometry={x: 1}
            )
    return model

All three agree to the integration tolerance. The forward sensitivities' cost grows with the number of parameters, the adjoint's doesn't, and the compiled adjoint is about two orders of magnitude faster still. For a few parameters (here: \(n \cdot m < 1000\)) forward sensitivities are faster, which is why auto keeps them there.

docs.title: Adjoint gradients¶
docs.text:
Forward sensitivities give the derivative of every simulated value with respect to every parameter. Gradient-based fitting usually needs much less: the gradient of one number, the loss, with respect to all parameters. For a loss \(L\) that depends on the simulation at a few time points, that gradient is a vector-Jacobian product

\[\frac{dL}{d\theta} = \sum_i \frac{\partial L}{\partial y(t_i)} \frac{\partial y(t_i)}{\partial \theta} = \sum_i w_i^\top S(t_i)\]

with the cotangents \(w_i = \partial L / \partial y(t_i)\).

Forward sensitivities compute all of \(S\), integrating \(n\) extra states per parameter. The adjoint method computes the product directly: it integrates an adjoint state \(\lambda\) backwards in time,

\[\frac{d\lambda}{dt} = -\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\top} \lambda, \qquad \lambda \mathrel{+}= w_i \text{ at every } t_i, \qquad \frac{dL}{d\theta} = \int_0^T \lambda^\top \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\, dt + \lambda(0)^\top \frac{\partial x_0}{\partial \theta}.\]

That is one forward and one backward solve, however many parameters there are. This is what makes fits with hundreds of parameters practical, e.g. the weights of neural networks in hybrid models.

cost per gradient best for finite differences \(2m\) simulations models that can't be differentiated forward sensitivities one solve with \(n(1 + m)\) states few parameters, residual Jacobians (least squares) adjoint one forward and one backward solve with \(n\) states many parameters, loss gradients

Both products \(\lambda^\top \partial f / \partial x\) and \(\lambda^\top \partial f / \partial \theta\) are generated symbolically in reverse mode, without forming Jacobians. The backward solve interpolates the forward trajectory instead of integrating the model backwards, which would be unstable for stiff models.

docs.title: A small example¶
docs.text: The linear chain \(x \to y \to \varnothing\) again, with weights on \(x\), \(y\) and the reaction v1 at four time points.

docs.title: Steady states¶
docs.text: At a steady state the adjoint of the implicit function theorem needs one linear solve, \(J^\top \mu = w\), for all parameters. Conserved quantities are fixed by the initial values, as for forward sensitivities.

docs.title: Protocols¶
docs.text: protocol_time_course differentiates a protocol simulation, whose steps set parameters. The adjoint runs backwards through the steps with each step's parameters; \(\lambda\) is continuous at the step ends. Forward sensitivities don't support protocols, so the alternative is finite differences, and auto uses adjoints from PROTOCOL_ADJOINT_THRESHOLD (3) parameters on.

docs.title: Loss gradients in fits¶
docs.text:
Fits get their derivatives from the runner. With derivatives="adjoint" the gradient of the loss comes from one adjoint solve, with the cotangents \(\partial L / \partial y\) of the chosen loss (standard scaling, replicates, GaussianNll weights and priors included). Residual Jacobians, which least-squares methods need, can't come from adjoints cheaply and still use forward sensitivities.

fit.loss_gradient evaluates the gradient a minimizer sees:

docs.title: When adjoints pay off¶
docs.text:
Forward sensitivities integrate \(n(1 + m)\) states with dense Jacobians of that size, adjoints cost about the same for any number of parameters \(m\). method="auto" therefore switches to adjoints from adjoint_sensitivities.ADJOINT_THRESHOLD (1000) variables × parameters on, the crossover measured on chains with an added neural-network-like layer.

The Native integrator runs the forward and the backward solve and the parameter quadrature in compiled code (Radau or LSODA, LLVM or wasm backend). It can't integrate forward sensitivities, so auto always uses the compiled adjoint with it. Models it can't compile fall back to the Python adjoint, and its CVODE methods to the variables × parameters rule.

Here is a model with \(n = 6\) states and a layer of 20 tanh units feeding back into every state, 266 parameters in total:

docs.title: Limitations¶
docs.text:
• Models with events use forward sensitivities (or finite differences); method="adjoint" raises.
  • Fits with a postprocess_fn use finite differences of the runner's results.
  • Models that can't be differentiated symbolically (e.g. neural-network surrogates) fall back to forward sensitivities, and from there to finite differences.

def proportional(k: float, s: float) -> float:
    return k * s
def constant(k: float) -> float: return k def proportional(k: float, s: float) -> float: return k * s

Next, we create our model.

For this, we first import the Model class from the mxlpy package.

In [3]: Copied! 
from mxlpy import Model

model = Model()
from mxlpy import Model model = Model()

We first add parameters to the model using .add_parameters({name: value}).

Note that the function returns our Model object again. This will be useful later, as we can chain multiple calls together.

In [4]: Copied! 
from mxlpy import Parameter, units

model = model.add_parameters(
    {
        "k1": 1,
        "k_1": Parameter(1, unit=units.mmol_s),
        "k_out": 1,
    }
)
from mxlpy import Parameter, units model = model.add_parameters( { "k1": 1, "k_1": Parameter(1, unit=units.mmol_s), "k_out": 1, } )

Next we add the dynamic variables S and P with their respective initial condition.

In [5]: Copied! 
model = model.add_variables({"S": 0, "P": 0})
model = model.add_variables({"S": 0, "P": 0})

Finally, we add the three reactions by using

.add_reaction(
    name,              # the internal name for the reaction
    fn=...,            # a python function to be evaluated
    args=[name, ...]   # the arguments passed to the python function
    stoichiometry={    # a mapping encoding how much the variable `name`
        name: value    # is changed by the reaction
    },
)

Attention There are a couple of points to note here. First, the function passed to fn here (and elsewhere) needs to be pickle-able Thus, lambda functions are not supported!

Second, the arguments defined with args are passed to fn by position, not by name. Thus, the order of arguments in args needs to match the order of arguments in fn

In [6]: Copied! 
model.add_reaction(
    "v0",
    fn=constant,
    args=["k1"],
    stoichiometry={"S": 1},  # produces one S
)
model.add_reaction(
    "v1",
    fn=proportional,
    args=["k_1", "S"],  # note that the order needs to match `proportional`
    stoichiometry={"S": -1, "P": 1},  # consumes one S and produces one P
)
model.add_reaction(
    "v2",
    fn=proportional,
    args=["k_out", "P"],  # note that the order needs to match `proportional`
    stoichiometry={"P": -1},  # exports one P
)

print(model.get_reaction_names())
model.add_reaction( "v0", fn=constant, args=["k1"], stoichiometry={"S": 1}, # produces one S ) model.add_reaction( "v1", fn=proportional, args=["k_1", "S"], # note that the order needs to match `proportional` stoichiometry={"S": -1, "P": 1}, # consumes one S and produces one P ) model.add_reaction( "v2", fn=proportional, args=["k_out", "P"], # note that the order needs to match `proportional` stoichiometry={"P": -1}, # exports one P ) print(model.get_reaction_names()) 
['v0', 'v1', 'v2']

Note, that we in general recommend to use a single function that returns the model instead of defining it globally. This allows us to quickly re-create the model whenever we need a fresh version of it. Below, we define the same model again, but inside a single function.

Note that we made use of operator chaining to avoid having to write model for every call.

So we can write Model.method1().method2()... instead of having to write

model.method1()
model.method2()

etc

In [7]: Copied! 
from mxlpy import Variable


def create_linear_chain_model() -> Model:
    return (
        Model()
        .add_parameters(
            {
                "k1": Parameter(1, unit=units.mmol_s),
                "k_1": Parameter(1, unit=units.per_second),
                "k_out": Parameter(1, unit=units.per_second),
            }
        )
        .add_variables(
            {
                "S": Variable(0, unit=units.mmol),
                "P": Variable(0, unit=units.mmol),
            }
        )
        .add_reaction(
            "v0",
            fn=constant,
            args=["k1"],
            stoichiometry={"S": 1},  # produces one S
            unit=units.mmol_s,
        )
        .add_reaction(
            "v1",
            fn=proportional,
            args=["k_1", "S"],  # note that the order needs to match `proportional`
            stoichiometry={"S": -1, "P": 1},  # consumes one S and produces one P
            unit=units.mmol_s,
        )
        .add_reaction(
            "v2",
            fn=proportional,
            args=["k_out", "P"],  # note that the order needs to match `proportional`
            stoichiometry={"P": -1},  # exports one P
            unit=units.mmol_s,
        )
    )
from mxlpy import Variable def create_linear_chain_model() -> Model: return ( Model() .add_parameters( { "k1": Parameter(1, unit=units.mmol_s), "k_1": Parameter(1, unit=units.per_second), "k_out": Parameter(1, unit=units.per_second), } ) .add_variables( { "S": Variable(0, unit=units.mmol), "P": Variable(0, unit=units.mmol), } ) .add_reaction( "v0", fn=constant, args=["k1"], stoichiometry={"S": 1}, # produces one S unit=units.mmol_s, ) .add_reaction( "v1", fn=proportional, args=["k_1", "S"], # note that the order needs to match `proportional` stoichiometry={"S": -1, "P": 1}, # consumes one S and produces one P unit=units.mmol_s, ) .add_reaction( "v2", fn=proportional, args=["k_out", "P"], # note that the order needs to match `proportional` stoichiometry={"P": -1}, # exports one P unit=units.mmol_s, ) )

We can then simulate the model by passing it to a Simulator and simulate a time series using .simulate(t_end). Finally, we can obtain the concentrations and fluxes using get_result.

While you can directly plot the pd.DataFrames, mxlpy supplies a variety of plots in the plot namespace that are worth checking out.

Note, that we explicitly checked whether the simulation failed.

Since there can be a multitude of reasons why a simulation might fail, we return a Result[Simulation | Exception] object, which you can use to investigate potential errors.

In contrast, if you are sure the simulation won't fail, and still want your code to be type-safe, you can use .unwrap_or_err().

result = Simulator(model).simulate(10).get_result().unwrap_or_err()

Note that these functions will raise an error if the simulation failed, which potentially might crash your programs.

docs.title: Model building basics¶
docs.text:
In the following you will learn how to build and simulate your first model using mxlpy.

This will allow you to create time courses and do steady-state analysis as shown below.

docs.title: Defining your first model¶
docs.text:
Let's say you want to model the following chemical network of a linear chain of reactions

\[ \Large \varnothing \xrightarrow{v_0} S \xrightarrow{v_1} P \xrightarrow{v_2} \varnothing \]

We can translate this into a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs)

\[\begin{align*} \frac{dS}{dt} &= v_0 - v_1 \\ \frac{dP}{dt} &= v_1 - v_2 \\ \end{align*} \]

Note that the rates \(v\) effect the variables by certain factors, known as stoichiometries. We can explicity write out these factors like this:

\[\begin{align*} \frac{dS}{dt} &= 1 \cdot v_0 -1 \cdot v_1 \\ \frac{dP}{dt} &= 1\cdot v_1 -1 \cdot v_2 \\ \end{align*} \]

In the example the stoichiometries are all \(1\) or \(-1\), however, they can have any real value. We can write out the stoichiometries using a stoichiometric matrix:

Variable \(v_0\) \(v_1\) \(v_2\) S 1 -1 0 P 0 1 -1

Which we can read as (ignoring the 0 entries):

  • S is produced by \(v_0\) and consumed by \(v_1\)
  • P is produced by \(v_1\) and consumed by \(v_2\)

Lastly we choose rate equations for each rate to get the flux vector \(v\)

\[\begin{align*} v_0 &= k_{in} \\ v_1 &= k_1 * S \\ v_2 &= k_{out} * P \\ \end{align*}\]

docs.title: Implementing your first model¶
docs.text: Now let's implement this first model in mxlpy. We start by creating the rate functions \(\textbf{v}\). Note that these should be general and re-usable whenever possible, to make your model clear to people reading it. Try to give these functions names that are meaningful to your audience, e.g. a rate function k * s could be named proportional or mass-action.

docs.title: Derived quantities¶
docs.text:
Frequently it makes sense to derive one quantity in a model from other quantities. This can be done for

  • parameters derived from other parameters
  • variables derived from parameters or other variables
  • stoichiometries derived from parameters or variables (more on this later)

mxlpy offers a unified interface for derived parameters and variables usign Model.add_derived().

docs.title: Introspection¶
docs.text:
If the simulation didn't show the expected results, it is usually a good idea to try to pinpoint the error. mxlpy offers a variety of methods to access intermediate results.

The first is to check whether all derived quantities were calculate correctly. For this, you can use the get_args method, which is named consistently with the args argument in all methods like add_reaction.

docs.title: CRUD¶
docs.text:
The model has a complete create, read, update, delete API for all it's elements. The methods and attributes are named consistenly, with add instead of create and get instead of read. Note that the elements itself are accessible as properties, e.g. .parameters which will return copies of the data. Only use the supplied methods to change the internal state of the model.

Here are some example methods and attributes for parameters

Functionality Parameters Create .add_parameter(), .add_parameters() Read .parameters, .get_parameter_names() Update .update_parameter(), .update_parameters(), .scale_parameter(), scale.parameters() Delete .remove_parameter(), .remove_parameters()

and variables

Functionality Variables Create .add_variable(), .add_variables() Read .variables, .get_variable_names(), get_initial_conditions() Update .update_variable(), .update_variables() Delete .remove_parameter(), .remove_parameters()

docs.title: Derived stoichiometries¶
docs.text:
To define derived stoichiometries can make them dependent on parameters in the model or use the Derived class as a value in the stoichiometries.

So instead of defining them like this

stoichiometry={"x": 1.0}

you can use

stoichiometry={"x": "stoich"}

or for more advanced uses you use the Derived class as the value

stoichiometry={"x": Derived(fn=constant, args=["stoich"])}

docs.title: Simulations: time courses¶
docs.text:
Time courses are simulations over time

You can obtain the time course of integration using the simulate method. There are two ways how you can define the time points this function returns.

  1. supply the end time t_end
  2. supply both end time and number of steps with t_end and steps

If you want to set the exact time points to be returned use simulate_time_course

simulate(t_end=10)
simulate(t_end=10, steps=10)
simulate_time_course(np.linspace(0, 10, 11))

docs.title: Inspecting the result object¶
docs.text: The object returned by the simulator has a couple of neat features

docs.title: Simulations: protocol time course¶
docs.text:
Protocols are used to make parameter changes discrete in time, such as turning a light on and off. This is useful reproducing experimental time courses where a parameter was changed at fixed time points.

The protocol is defined as a pandas.DataFrame using pd.Timedelta values as in index, and the parameter values at the respective time interval as values.

pd.Timedelta p1 p2 0 days 00:00:01 1 0 0 days 00:00:03 2 1 0 days 00:00:06 1 2

You can use as many parameters as you want.

Note mxlpy assigns one second of the Timedelta to one time unit of the integration. mxlpy does not take into account whether your integration might use a different time unit.

For convenience, we supply the make_protocol function, which takes in a pair of the duration of the time-step on the respective parameter values.

docs.title: Simulations: steady-state¶
docs.text:
A steady-state describes a state at which the concentrations of the system don't change anymore (also called fixed points).

You can simulate until the model reaches a steady-state using the simulate_to_steady_state method.

docs.title: Visualizing model structure¶
docs.text:
mxlpy can render a model's reaction network as a directed graph using plot.network using networkx under the hood.

Variables are displayed as circles and reactions as squares. Solid arrows show a stoichiometric edge (e.g. substrate → reaction or reaction → product) and dashed edges show modifiers (variable appears in args but not in stoichiometry)

docs.title: SBML¶
docs.text:
The systems biology markup language (SBML) is a widely used file format for sharing models between different software packages and programming languages.

mxlpy supports reading and writing sbml models using the sbml.read and sbml.write functions.

docs.title: MIRIAM annotations¶
docs.text:
To make a model interoperable with biological databases (and submittable to the BioModels Database), you can attach standardized ontology identifiers (UniProt, ChEBI, KEGG, GO, …) to its components using the Annotation class.

Each Annotation pairs an identifiers.org uri with a MIRIAM predicate (default "is"). The annotations argument is accepted by every add_* and update_* method as a single Annotation or an iterable, and annotate_model attaches model-level annotations.

Components use biological qualifiers (bqbiol, e.g. is, hasPart, isVersionOf, occursIn, …), while the model itself uses model qualifiers (bqmodel, e.g. is, isDerivedFrom, isDescribedBy).

Annotations are stored on the model and serialised as <annotation><rdf:RDF> blocks on export; sbml.read parses them back, giving full round-trip support.

docs.title: Time-dependent reactions¶
docs.text: You can use the special name time to refer to the actual integration time in the rare case a reaction or module depends on it explicitly. This is why the methods get_args, get_fluxes etc. also take an additional time argument.

docs.title: Derived parameters and variables¶
docs.text:
Internally mxlpy differentiates between derived parameters and derived variables. This differentiation is just-in-time before any calculation and thus might change if you change the nature of a parameter / variable.

If you are interested in which category mxlpy has placed the derived quantities, you can access .derived_parameters and .derived_variables as well.

docs.title: Derived initial conditions¶
docs.text: MxlPy supports initial assignments. These are essentially derived values which are just calculated once.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text: You can add references to data using add_data. That way, you can, for example, dynamically derive aggregates over them.

docs.title: Bayesian inference (MCMC)¶
docs.text:
A fit returns the single parameter set that best describes the data. It doesn't tell you how well the data constrain each parameter: often a whole range of values fits almost equally well.

mxlpy can instead sample the posterior distribution of the parameters given the data, using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). From the samples you get credible intervals, correlations between parameters and the uncertainty of predictions.

The posterior combines two ingredients:

  • the likelihood of the data: the data are assumed to be the model's prediction plus Gaussian measurement noise with a known standard deviation sigma
  • a prior per sampled parameter: what you know about the parameter before seeing the data, given as a distribution from mxlpy.distributions

docs.title: Creating synthetic data¶
docs.text: As in the fitting tutorial, we create noisy synthetic data from a model with known parameters.

docs.title: Sampling the posterior¶
docs.text:
fit.mcmc_time_course takes the data, a prior for every parameter to sample and the noise level sigma. The keys of prior are the sampled parameters; all other parameters keep their model values.

Rate constants are positive and can span orders of magnitude, so a log-normal prior is a natural choice. Parameters whose prior lives on (0, inf) are sampled as their logarithm internally, which makes the sampler much more efficient; all results are reported in natural units.

Several independent chains run in parallel. A seed makes the samples reproducible.

docs.title: Checking convergence¶
docs.text:
Before interpreting the samples, check that the chains have converged to the same distribution.

  • R-hat compares the chains with each other; values below about 1.01 indicate convergence
  • the effective sample size (ESS) estimates how many independent samples the correlated chain samples are worth; a few hundred are enough for intervals
  • the acceptance rate of the sampler should be roughly between 0.15 and 0.5

docs.title: Credible intervals¶
docs.text: credible_intervals gives equal-tailed intervals containing level of the posterior mass, and the median.

docs.title: Prediction uncertainty¶
docs.text: Simulating the model for a random subset of the posterior samples propagates the parameter uncertainty to the predictions.

docs.title: Steady states and protocols¶
docs.text:
The steady-state and protocol variants work the same way. sigma can also be given per data column (or entry, for steady states) as a pandas.Series, or per data point as a pandas.DataFrame. Missing data (NaN) are ignored.

Here the steady state only constrains the ratios of the rate constants, so we fix k1 and only sample the others.

docs.title: Priors¶
docs.text: Any distribution with a log_pdf and a positive_support (the mxlpy.distributions.Prior protocol) can be a prior, e.g. a Normal for a parameter that can be negative (it is then sampled linearly), or a Uniform for hard bounds.

docs.title: Starting point¶
docs.text: By default the chains start (slightly spread out) at the model's current parameter values. Starting from a previous fit with x0 saves warm-up time.

docs.title: Sampler¶
docs.text:
The default sampler is fit.AdaptiveMetropolis (Haario et al. 2001): during a warm-up it adapts the covariance of its Gaussian proposals to the shape of the posterior, then it samples with the proposal frozen. The warm-up is discarded and defaults to as many steps as samples.

Any callable following the fit.McmcSampler protocol can be passed as sampler.

docs.text:

import numpy as np

from mxlpy import Model, Simulator, fit, fns, plot
from mxlpy.carousel import Carousel, ReactionTemplate


def get_sir() -> Model:
    """Create a simple SIR model."""
    return (
        Model()
        .add_variables({"s": 0.9, "i": 0.1, "r": 0.0})
        .add_parameters({"beta": 0.2, "gamma": 0.1})
        .add_reaction(
            "infection",
            fns.mass_action_2s,
            args=["s", "i", "beta"],
            stoichiometry={"s": -1, "i": 1},
        )
        .add_reaction(
            "recovery",
            fns.mass_action_1s,
            args=["i", "gamma"],
            stoichiometry={"i": -1, "r": 1},
        )
    )


carousel = Carousel(
    get_sir(),
    {
        "infection": [
            ReactionTemplate(fn=fns.mass_action_2s, args=["s", "i", "beta"]),
            ReactionTemplate(
                fn=fns.michaelis_menten_2s,
                args=["s", "i", "beta", "km_bs", "km_bi"],
                additional_parameters={"km_bs": 0.1, "km_bi": 1.0},
            ),
        ],
        "recovery": [
            ReactionTemplate(fn=fns.mass_action_1s, args=["i", "gamma"]),
            ReactionTemplate(
                fn=fns.michaelis_menten_1s,
                args=["i", "gamma", "km_gi"],
                additional_parameters={"km_gi": 0.1},
            ),
        ],

docs.title: Comparisons¶
docs.text: mxlpy provides simple routines to numerically compare two models. For this, we use the compare module.

docs.title: Steady-states¶
docs.text: You can compare the steady-states of two models using the compare_steady_states function.

docs.title: Time courses¶
docs.text: For comparing time courses, you can use the compare_time_courses function. This returns a TimeCourseComparison object, which you can directly use to plot for example the relative differences of variables or fluxes.

docs.title: Protocol time courses¶
docs.text: For comparing protocol time courses, you can use the protocol_time_courses function. This returns a ProtocolComparison object, which you can directly use to plot for example the relative differences of variables or fluxes.

from dataclasses import dataclass

from mxlpy.types import InitialAssignment


def one_div(x: float) -> float:
    return 1.0 / x


def minus_one_div(x: float) -> float:
    return -1.0 / x


def times_frac(top: float, btm: float, x: float) -> float:
    return top / btm * x


def ma_1s_1p_keq(s1: float, p1: float, kf: float, keq: float) -> float:
    return kf * (s1 - p1 / keq)
from dataclasses import dataclass from mxlpy import Model, Simulator, fns, plot from mxlpy.types import InitialAssignment def one_div(x: float) -> float: return 1.0 / x def minus_one_div(x: float) -> float: return -1.0 / x def times_frac(top: float, btm: float, x: float) -> float: return top / btm * x def ma_1s_1p_keq(s1: float, p1: float, kf: float, keq: float) -> float: return kf * (s1 - p1 / keq) In [2]: Copied! 
@dataclass
class VarNames:
    amount: str
    conc: str


def add_cvar(
    model: Model,
    name: str,
    compartment: str,
    initial: float,
    *,
    initial_is_amount: bool = True,
    amount_prefix: str = "n_",
    conc_prefix: str = "c_",
) -> VarNames:
    amount = f"{amount_prefix}{name}_{compartment}"
    if not initial_is_amount:
        # FIXME: rewrite initial assignment to take in float?
        model.add_parameter(init_c := f"c_{name}_init", initial)
        model.add_variable(
            amount,
            InitialAssignment(fn=fns.mul, args=[init_c, compartment]),
        )
    else:
        model.add_variable(amount, initial)
    model.add_derived(
        conc := f"{conc_prefix}{name}_{compartment}",
        fn=fns.div,
        args=[amount, compartment],
    )
    return VarNames(amount, conc)


m = Model()
m.add_parameters({"c1": 2.0, "c2": 4.0})

# Add a compartmentalised variable with an initial amount
x_c1 = add_cvar(m, "x", compartment="c1", initial=1.5)

# Add a compartmentalised variable with an initial concentration
x_c2 = add_cvar(m, "x", compartment="c2", initial=1.5, initial_is_amount=False)

args = m.get_args()

print("Concentrations", args.loc[[x_c1.conc, x_c2.conc]], sep="\n", end="\n\n")

def rate_factor(rxn_place: float, k: float, compartment: float) -> float:
    return rxn_place * k / compartment


def add_rate_factor(
    model: Model,
    base: str,
    value: float,
    rxn_compartment: str,
    cpd_compartment: str,
    k_prefix: str = "k_",
    f_prefix: str = "f_",
) -> str:
    model.add_parameter(k := f"{k_prefix}{base}", value)
    f = f"{f_prefix}{base}"
    model.add_derived(
        f,
        fn=rate_factor,
        args=[rxn_compartment, k, cpd_compartment],
    )
    return f


m = Model()
m.add_parameters({"c1": 2.0, "a1": 4.0})
rf = add_rate_factor(m, "r1", 1.0, rxn_compartment="a1", cpd_compartment="c1")

m.get_args().loc[rf]

docs.title: Compartmental models¶
docs.text:
We follow the recommendations by Hofmeyr (2020) (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biosystems.2020.104203) when it comes to compartmentalisation. That is, describe compartmentalised variables in terms of amounts instead of concentration and scale kinetic constants by the compartment to yield rate factors.

Depending on your use case, your experimental data might be described as concentrations and communication is also prefered in concentrations.

mxlpy provides various ways of how you can automate that mapping

  • use Derived variables and parameters to obtain concentrations from the amounts.
  • use InitialAssignments to calculate initial amounts in case your data is given in concentrations

Below we define convenience functions for exactly that, to reduce boilerplate code

docs.title: Single compartment¶
docs.text:
In case all your reactions happen in the volume of the same compartment, you don't need to change anything.

Whether your variables describe an amount or a concentration does not matter, the equations are identical.

Here we use standard reversible mass-action kinetics, once formulated explicitly with forward and backward kinetic constants and once using the equilibrium constant.

\[\begin{align*} v &= k_f x - k_r y \\ &= k_f \left( x - \frac{y}{K_{eq}} \right)\\ \end{align*}\]

docs.title: Single compartment - at membrane¶
docs.text: \[\begin{align*} v &= {\color{purple} A} \left( k_f \frac{n_x}{{\color{cyan}C_1} } - k_r \frac{n_y}{{\color{cyan}C_1}} \right) \\ &= f_f n_x - f_r n_y \\ &= f_f \left( n_x - \frac{n_y}{K_{eq}} \right)\\ \end{align*}\]

docs.title: Single compartment - on membrane¶
docs.text:
This special case depends only on the area of the membrane, not on the volume of the compartment

\[\begin{align*} v &= {\color{purple} A} \left( k_f \frac{n_x}{{\color{purple} A} } - k_r \frac{n_y}{{\color{purple} A} } \right) \\ &= f_f n_x - f_r n_y \\ &= f_f \left( n_x - \frac{n_y}{K_{eq}} \right)\\ \end{align*}\]

docs.text: \[\begin{align*} v &= {\color{purple} A} \left( k_f \frac{n_x}{{\color{cyan} C_1}} - k_r \frac{n_y}{{\color{coral} C_2}} \right) \\ &= f_f n_x - f_r n_y \\ &= f_f \left( n_x - \frac{n_y}{K_{eq}} \right)\\ \end{align*}\]

The composed model behaves exactly like a hand-written one: x relaxes towards its steady state k_in / k_out = 1.0.

compose accepts any number of models (compose(a, b, c, ...)), folding them left-to-right, so you can stack several modules in a single call.

docs.title: Model composition¶
docs.text:
Large models are easier to build, test and maintain when assembled from smaller, independently validated submodels — for example a metabolic core plus a separate regulatory layer.

mxlpy.compose merges two or more Model objects into a single new model. Components are identified by name across the whole namespace (variables, parameters, derived quantities, reactions, readouts, surrogates and data), and the input models are never mutated.

from mxlpy import compose

full_model = compose(submodel_a, submodel_b)

docs.title: Merging disjoint submodels¶
docs.text: If two models share no names, compose simply returns a new model containing the union of all their components.

docs.title: Name conflicts¶
docs.text: By default any name defined in more than one model is treated as a conflict and raises a ValueError. This protects you from silently merging two unrelated components that happen to share a name.

docs.title: Sharing components on purpose¶
docs.text: To deliberately connect submodels through a shared component — here the species x, produced by one submodel and consumed by the other — pass raise_on_conflict=False. A warning is emitted for each overridden name and the component from the later model wins.

The SIRD model for example differentiates between recovered and deceased individuals.

docs.title: SIR and SIRD models¶
docs.text:
In epidemiology, compartmental models are often applied to model infectious diseases.

Common compartments include ones for Susceptible, Infectious and Recovered individuals, which are included in the SIR model.

In this model there are two transitions (reactions in mxlpy) between those compartments.

  • susceptible individuals can become infected by contact with an infected person: \(\beta S I\)
  • infected people can recover with a rate proportional: \(\gamma I\)

These transitions are scaled by the average number of contacts per person per time (\(\beta\)) and the inverse of the average infection time \(\gamma\).

By default, mxlpy will apply standard scaling to all fitting functions.

Specifically, it will calculate loss_fn(data - data.mean()) / data.std(), (pred - data.mean()) / data.std()).

Rate constants often span several orders of magnitude. With transform="log" (or a per-parameter mapping like {"k1": "log"}) the minimizer works in log10 space, which keeps parameters positive and makes steps scale-free. Log-transformed parameters without explicit bounds get the bounds (1e-6, 1e6). Transforms are opt-in, since a quasi-Newton method like L-BFGS-B can overshoot by a factor of ten on its first log-space step.

Fit.loss is the loss of the data alone and Fit.penalty the prior's contribution at the optimum, so multi-start fits pick their best fit by fit_result.objective = loss + penalty. Penalties coupling several parameters (e.g. for regularising differences between conditions) implement the fit.Penalty protocol and are passed as penalty=.
 
With the Native integrator's llvm backend installed (mxlpy[native]), LeastSquaresMinimizer(method="lm", backend="native") runs the whole Levenberg-Marquardt fit in compiled code: the model, its sensitivities and the fit loop. It usually is several times faster than the scipy backend, and integrates with the method and tolerances of the runner's Native integrator (Radau or LSODA). Like any method="lm" fit it ignores bounds, so use transform="log" for parameters that have to stay positive. Fits it can't compile (e.g. with a postprocess_fn or fitted initial values) fall back to the scipy backend with a warning.

docs.title: Fitting¶
docs.text:
Almost every model at some point needs to be fitted to experimental data to be validated.

mxlpy offers highly customisable local and global routines for fitting either time series or steady-states.

The entire set of currently supported routines is

Single model, single data

  • steady_state
  • time_course
  • protocol_time_course

Single model, single data, multiple initial guesses (a.k.a. multi-start optimisation)

  • group_steady_state
  • group_time_course
  • group_protocol_time_course

Multiple model, single data

  • ensemble_steady_state
  • ensemble_time_course
  • ensemble_protocol_time_course

A carousel is a special case of an ensemble, where the general structure (e.g. stoichiometries) is the same, while the reactions kinetics can vary

  • carousel_steady_state
  • carousel_time_course
  • carousel_protocol_time_course

Multiple model, multiple data

  • joint_steady_state
  • joint_time_course
  • joint_protocol_time_course

Multiple model, multiple data, multiple methods

Here we also allow to run different methods (e.g. steady-state vs time courses) for each combination of model:data.

  • joint_mixed

docs.title: Minimizers¶
docs.text:
• LocalScipyMinimizer, including common methods such as Nelder-Mead or L-BFGS-B
  • GlobalScipyMinimizer, including common methods such as basin hopping or dual annealing

For this tutorial we are going to use the fit module to optimise our parameter values and the plot module to plot some results.

Let's get started!

docs.title: Creating synthetic data¶
docs.text:
Normally, you would fit your model to experimental data. Here, for the sake of simplicity, we will generate some synthetic data.

Checkout the basics tutorial if you need a refresher on building and simulating models.

docs.title: Steady-states¶
docs.text:
For the steady-state fit we need two inputs:

  1. the steady state data, which we supply as a pandas.Series
  2. an initial parameter guess

The fitting routine will compare all data contained in that series to the model output.

Note that the data both contains concentrations and fluxes!

docs.title: Time course¶
docs.text:
For the time course fit we need again need two inputs

  1. the time course data, which we supply as a pandas.DataFrame
  2. an initial parameter guess

The fitting routine will create data at every time points specified in the DataFrame and compare all of them.

Other than that, the same rules of the steady-state fitting apply.

docs.title: Protocol time courses¶
docs.text:
For the protocol time course fit we need three inputs

  1. an initial parameter guess
  2. the time course data, which we supply as a pandas.DataFrame
  3. the protocol, which we supply as a pandas.DataFrame

Note that the parameter given by the protocol cannot be fitted anymore

You can use the make_protocol function to create a protocol (see above).

The protocol DataFrame should preferrably use a pd.TimedeltaIndex and is interpreted as "use the parameter values of that row until the given end point."

Here a second corresponds to a unit of simulation time, regardless of model time scale.

mxlpy will attempt to convert other indices, again assuming that a second in your data corresponds to a second of simulation time.

docs.title: Group fitting (multi-start optimisation)¶
docs.text:
mxlpy supports group fitting, which is a single-model, single-data approach where the same model is fitted to the same data from many different initial parameter guesses.

This is exactly what is commonly called multi-start (or multistart) optimisation: each row of the p0 DataFrame is one start, the starts are run in parallel, and a GroupFit is returned. Use get_best_fit() to retrieve the best result and get_losses() to inspect the loss of every start.

A convenient way to generate diverse start guesses is mxlpy.distributions.sample, as shown in the monte-carlo combination further down.

docs.title: Time course¶
docs.text: Time course fits are adjusted just the same

docs.title: Protocol time course¶
docs.text: As are protocol time courses

docs.title: Combining with monte-carlo approaches¶
docs.text: An especially useful combination is combining group fitting with the monte-carlo capabilities of mxlpy to quickly get multiple fits from randomly selected initial conditions

docs.title: Ensemble fitting¶
docs.text:
mxlpy supports ensemble fitting, which is a multi-model single data approach, where shared parameters will be applied to all models at the same time.

Here you supply an iterable of models instead of just one, otherwise the API stays the same.

docs.title: Time course¶
docs.text: Time course fits are adjusted just the same

docs.title: Protocol time course¶
docs.text: As are protocol time courses

docs.title: Joint fitting¶
docs.text: Next, we support joint fitting, which is a combined multi-model multi-data approach, where shared parameters will be applied to all models at the same time

docs.title: Advanced topics / customisation¶
docs.text:
All fitting routines internally are build in a way that they will call a tree of functions.

  • minimizer
    • residual_fn
      • integrator
      • loss_fn

You can therefore use dependency injection to overwrite the minimisation function, the loss function, the residual function and the integrator if need be.

docs.title: Gradient-based fitting¶
docs.text:
With the built-in residual functions, fits give minimizers the exact gradient, the residual Jacobian and a Gauss-Newton Hessian, computed only when a minimizer asks for them. The runner computes them, so runner=KineticRunner(derivatives=...) chooses how:

  • derivatives="auto" (the default) integrates the forward sensitivities dS/dt = J·S + ∂f/∂θ alongside the model (see parameter sensitivities); for steady-state fits it uses the implicit function theorem. Models that can't be differentiated symbolically (surrogates, events, the Native or Diffrax integrators) fall back to finite differences, as do protocol fits and fits with a postprocess_fn.
  • derivatives="finite_difference" always uses central finite differences, derivatives="forward" warns when it can't be used.

Gradient methods of LocalScipyMinimizer (e.g. L-BFGS-B, the default for more than one parameter) and FixedNMinimizer receive jac=; methods using a Hessian like method="trust-constr" also get the Gauss-Newton approximation of the Hessian (for the rmse and mean_squared losses). LeastSquaresMinimizer wraps scipy.optimize.least_squares (method="trf"|"dogbox"|"lm") and works directly on the residual vector, which usually converges in far fewer simulations.

docs.title: Priors and maximum-a-posteriori estimation¶
docs.text:
Prior knowledge about parameters, e.g. literature values from mxlpy.parameterise, can enter a point fit as prior={name: distribution}, the same mapping fit.mcmc_* takes. The fit then minimises loss + Σ penalty, where each penalty is the negative log density of the prior: Normal and LogNormal pull towards their centre, SoftBounds only penalises values outside a range (a smooth alternative to hard bounds), Laplace is an L1 penalty. Parameters without a prior are unpenalised.

Distributions defined on a log scale (LogNormal, LogUniform, SoftBounds(log=True)) are penalised on log(θ), so LogNormal(np.log(0.5), 0.2) pulls towards 0.5 and LogUniform is flat. The penalty doesn't depend on transform, so neither does the optimum.

The penalty is only on the same scale as the loss for a likelihood: with loss_fn=fit.GaussianNll(sigma), the negative log-likelihood of Gaussian measurement noise with standard deviation sigma (a scalar, one per observable or one per data point), the fit is a proper maximum-a-posteriori estimate. With heuristic losses like the default rmse the prior acts as a regularisation, whose strength you set with penalty=fit.PriorPenalty(prior, weight=...). LeastSquaresMinimizer minimises exactly the same loss + penalty, which needs a loss that is a sum of squares (GaussianNll or mean_squared); for other losses use e.g. LocalScipyMinimizer.

docs.title: Custom loss function¶
docs.text: You can change the loss function that is being passed to the minimsation function using the loss_fn keyword. Depending on the use case (time course vs steady state) this function will be passed two pandas DataFrames or Series.

docs.title: Post-processing the simulation¶
docs.text:
Derived values and readouts are calculated per time point, so quantities that depend on the whole time course (e.g. NPQ, which normalises the maximal fluorescence of every pulse by the first one) can't be expressed in the model itself. For these you can pass a postprocess_fn to every fitting routine. It receives the combined simulation result (variables, derived values, readouts and fluxes) at the time points of the data and has to return a DataFrame containing the data columns, which is then compared to the data by the loss function.

Here, for example, we fit to data that was normalised by its last value.

docs.title: Custom integrator¶
docs.text:
How the model is simulated during fitting is configured by a runner (see the integrator configuration). You can change the default integrator to an integrator of your choice by passing a runner with a partial application of the class of any of the existing ones.

Here, for example, we choose the Scipy solver suite and set the default relative and absolute tolerances to 1e-6 respectively.

docs.title: Parameter sensitivities¶
docs.text:
Global sensitivity analysis asks how much each parameter matters across a whole range of values. The complementary, local question is: how does every simulated value change when a parameter changes a little, right here? That is the derivative

\[S_{ij}(t) = \frac{\partial y_i(t)}{\partial \theta_j}\]

of every variable, derived quantity and reaction \(y_i\) with respect to every parameter (or initial value) \(\theta_j\). These forward sensitivities are what gradient-based fitting, Fisher-information analyses and identifiability checks are built on.

MxlPy computes them by solving the sensitivity equations alongside the model,

\[\frac{dS}{dt} = J\,S + \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}, \qquad S(0) = \frac{\partial x_0}{\partial \theta},\]

where both the Jacobian \(J = \partial f / \partial x\) and \(\partial f / \partial \theta\) are generated symbolically from the model. This needs a single (larger) simulation instead of one extra simulation per parameter, and is as accurate as the integrator.

docs.title: A small example¶
docs.text: A linear chain \(x \to y \to \varnothing\) with mass-action kinetics.

docs.title: Steady states¶
docs.text: At a steady state the sensitivities follow from the implicit function theorem, \(J\,\partial x^* / \partial \theta = -\partial f / \partial \theta\), without integrating anything. Conserved quantities make \(J\) singular; their totals are then fixed by the initial values, which MxlPy takes into account.

docs.title: When the model can't be differentiated symbolically¶
docs.text:
Forward sensitivities need every rate function to be convertible to sympy. Models with e.g. neural-network surrogates or functions that can't be parsed automatically fall back to central finite differences (two extra simulations per parameter) and log a warning. You can also choose explicitly with method="forward" or method="finite_difference".

Finite differences are only as accurate as the integrator allows: a too small step amplifies the integration error. The default relative step displacement=1e-3 suits the default tolerances of 1e-8.

docs.title: Explicit initial values, outputs and runners¶
docs.text:
Pass explicit initial values or select only some outputs:

forward_sensitivities.time_course(model, time_points, ["k1"], y0={"x": 1.0, "y": 0.0}, outputs=["v1"])

When y0 isn't given, the initial values are taken from the model, so initial assignments depending on the parameters are differentiated as well.

Runners provide the same with their own integrator and steady-state settings, which is where fits get their derivatives from:

runner = KineticRunner(derivatives="auto", displacement=1e-3)
runner.time_course_sensitivities(model, time_points, ["k1"])
runner.steady_state_sensitivities(model, ["kf"])

!!! note The Native and Diffrax integrators compile the model themselves and use finite-difference sensitivities.

For the gradient of a loss with many parameters, adjoint gradients are much cheaper: one forward and one backward solve, whatever the number of parameters.

docs.title: Integrator configuration¶
docs.text:
You can explicitly control which integrator is used for the simulations. As all integrators have different settings, changing them is done on the integrator object itself, which can be found at Simulator().integrator.

By default, the first available of these integrators is used:

  1. Assimulo (CVODE, installable from conda-forge)
  2. Sundials (CVODE via the official sundials4py bindings, pip install mxlpy[sundials])
  3. Scipy (LSODA)

Assimulo and Sundials run the same solver with the same default settings. However, that package currenlty requires installation via conda-forge. If mxlpy was installed from pypi, this package is not available and mxlpy will fall back to the Scipy package. Thus, when setting integrator settings you should always check which integrator you are actually working with, as this otherwise might lead bugs on other systems.

docs.title: Sundials¶
docs.text: Sundials wraps CVODE from the SUNDIALS suite. It needs the optional sundials extra (pip install mxlpy[sundials]), which has wheels for Linux x86_64, macOS and Windows x64. Use method="BDF" (default) for stiff and method="Adams" for non-stiff problems.

docs.title: Scans, fits and other routines¶
docs.text:
Routines like scan.*, fit.*, mc.* and mca.* don't take a Simulator, but a runner, which describes how each model is simulated. A runner holds the integrator as well as the settings of the steady-state search, so you configure them in one place for every routine.

There is one runner per model builder: KineticRunner for the default Model, OdeRunner for an OdeModelBuilder and EvaluationRunner for a SteadyStateModelBuilder. If no runner is passed, the default runner of the model builder is used.

docs.title: Native integrator¶
docs.text:
Native compiles a model and runs a C solver outside Python, which makes simulate typically 50-200x faster than with Scipy. Derived values, reactions and readouts are compiled too, on first read of the results, with the Python path as a fallback for any that can't be. It only works for models that can be represented symbolically, and raises NativeLoweringError for any other. It isn't installed by default, and there are two backends:

  • pip install "mxlpy[native]": llvmlite and a compiled solver. The fastest, needing a wheel for your platform.
  • pip install "mxlpy[native-wasm]": wasmtime only, more portable, about 1.2-3x slower than native.
from functools import partial
from mxlpy import Native, Simulator

Simulator(model, integrator=Native).simulate(100)
Simulator(model, integrator=partial(Native, rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-10)).simulate(100)

The first simulation of a model compiles it, usually in well under a second. Changing parameters doesn't recompile. Events aren't supported.

The default method is Radau, for stiff models. partial(Native, method="LSODA") uses LSODA instead, which switches between non-stiff and stiff methods by itself. It's the same C code Scipy(method="LSODA") runs, and on non-stiff models it can be faster than Radau. method="CVODE_BDF" (stiff) and method="CVODE_Adams" (non-stiff) use SUNDIALS' CVODE, the solver Assimulo runs, so they give the same results without needing conda.

partial(Native, reuse_jacobian=True) (Radau only) reuses Jacobians for longer. That can be about twice as fast on larger stiff models, but error can rise noticeably on some small models, and it's too rough for fits that use finite differences, so keep it off for fitting.

docs.title: Labeled models¶
docs.text:
Labelled models allow explicitly mapping the transitions between isotopomers variables. This, for example, allows building models of the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle, in which each carbon atom can be labelled individually:

mxlpy includes a LabelMapper that takes

  • a model
  • a dictionary mapping the variables to the amount of label positions they have
  • a transition map

to auto-generate all possible 2^n variants of the variables and reaction transitions between them.

As an example let's take triose phosphate isomerase, which catalyzes the interconversion of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (GAP) and dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP). As illustrated below, in the case of the forward reaction the first and last carbon atoms are swapped

So DHAP(1) is build from GAP(3), DHAP(2) from GAP(2) and DHAP(3) from GAP(1). We notate this using normal 0-based indexing as follows

label_maps = {"TPIf": [2, 1, 0]}

docs.title: Linear label mapper¶
docs.text: The LabelMapper makes no assumptions about the state of the model, which causes a lot of complexity. In steady-state however, the space of possible solutions is reduced and the labelling dynamics can be represented by a set of linear differential equations. See Sokol and Portais 2015 for the theory of dynamic label propagation under the stationary assumption.

docs.title: External & initial labels¶
docs.text: In the case of open models, we make the assumption that there is a static pool of external labels. For example, this could be the labelled portion of ambient carbon dioxide. We denote that external label pool with EXT and by default set the value 1.0 to it, which means that it is fully labelled.

docs.title: Metabolic control analysis¶
docs.text:
Metabolic control analysis answers the question: what happens to the concentrations and fluxes if I slightly perturb the system? It is thus a local measurement about which reactions hold the most control.

The most common measurements are elasticities and response coefficients. The main difference between them is that response coefficients are calculated at steady-state, while elasticities can be calculated at every arbitrary state.

All the required functionality can be found in the mxlpy.mca module.

As an example, we will use the upper glycolysis model from the Systems Biology textbook by Klipp et al. (2005).

docs.title: Variable elasticities¶
docs.text:
Variable elasticities are the sensitivity of reactions to a small change in the concentration of a variable. They are not a steady-state measurement and can be calculated for any arbitrary state.

Both the concs and variables arguments are optional. If concs is not supplied, the routine will use the initial conditions from the model. If variables is not supplied, the elasticities will be calculated for all variables.

docs.title: Parameter elasticities¶
docs.text:
Similarly, parameter elasticities are the sensitivity of reactions to a small change in the concentration of a variable. They are not a steady-state measurement and can be calculated for any arbitrary state.

Both the concs and parameters arguments are optional. If concs is not supplied, the routine will use the initial conditions from the model. If parameters is not supplied, the elasticities will be calculated for all parameters.

docs.title: Response coefficients¶
docs.text:
Response coefficients show the sensitivity of variables and reactions at steady-state to a small change in a parameter.

If the parameter is proportional to the rate, they are also called control coefficients.

Calculation of these is run in parallel by default.

docs.title: Time-dependent MCA¶
docs.text:
Response coefficients and elasticities aren't restricted to steady states. Passing time_points gives them along the trajectory starting from the initial conditions (or variables): how every variable and flux at every time point responds to a change of a parameter (Ingalls & Sauro 2003). They come from integrating the forward sensitivities alongside the model, i.e. a single simulation for all parameters.

The rows of the result are then indexed by (time, output), so rc.variables.loc[t] gives all variable responses at time t, and rc.for_parameter(name) a time × output table ready for plotting. Normalised coefficients are undefined where an output is zero, e.g. for variables starting at zero, which is why the time points below start just after 0.

docs.title: Steady-state stability¶
docs.text:
After finding a steady state you can classify its local stability from the eigenvalues of the Jacobian.

steady_state_stability evaluates the symbolic Jacobian at the given state, computes eigenvalues with numpy.linalg.eigvals, and returns a SteadyStateStability object:

Field Description eigenvalues Complex Jacobian eigenvalues spectral_abscissa Largest real part — negative ⟺ stable is_stable True when all real parts are negative has_oscillatory True when any eigenvalue has nonzero imaginary part classification "stable node" | "stable spiral" | "unstable node" | "unstable spiral" | "saddle point" | "centre" | "non-hyperbolic"

docs.title: Supply-demand rate characteristics¶
docs.text:
Where the analyses above are local (a small perturbation around a single state), rate characteristics show the global picture: how the reactions that produce and consume a metabolite respond across its whole concentration range.

rate_characteristics clamps a chosen variable to a logarithmically spaced range around its steady-state concentration, recomputes the steady state of the remaining variables at each point, and collects the fluxes of the reactions that produce it (supply) and consume it (demand). The intersection of total supply and total demand is the steady state — plotting both curves places that operating point in the context of the full range.

Reactions are classified structurally from the stoichiometry: a positive coefficient marks a supply reaction, a negative one a demand reaction. The scan spans [ss / min_factor, ss * max_factor] with n_points log-spaced samples.

The result exposes:

Attribute / method Description supply_fluxes / demand_fluxes Per-reaction fluxes vs. the clamped concentration (one column per reaction) total_supply / total_demand Summed supply / demand flux steady_state_conc Concentration of the variable at the original steady state plot_supply_demand() Total supply and demand on a single log-log axis plot() Three-panel summary: total supply vs. demand, per-reaction supply, per-reaction demand

Here we scan F6P, which is produced by two reactions (v3, v5) and consumed by one (v4).

docs.title: Normalisation¶
docs.text:
By default the elasticities and response coefficients are normalised, so e.g. for the response coefficients the following is calculated:

\[C^J_{v_i} = \left( \frac{dJ}{dp} \frac{p}{J} \right) \bigg/ \left( \frac{\partial v_i}{\partial p}\frac{p}{v_i} \right)\]

You can also obtain the non-normalised coefficients, by setting normalized=False, which amounts to the following calculation:

\[C^J_{v_i} = \left( \frac{dJ}{dp} \frac{p}{J} \right)\]

docs.title: Forward sensitivities and finite differences¶
docs.text:
We wrote above that we slightly change the value, but by how much exactly? By default, not at all: mxlpy computes the response coefficients from the forward sensitivities of the steady state. The implicit function theorem gives the derivatives of the steady state w.r.t. all parameters from a single steady-state simulation and one linear solve, \(J \, \partial x^* / \partial p = -\partial f / \partial p\), with both derivatives generated symbolically from the model. This is exact and needs far fewer simulations than perturbing every parameter.

Models that can't be differentiated symbolically (e.g. neural-network surrogates) fall back to central finite differences, changing every parameter to \[\textrm{value} \cdot \left(1 \pm \Delta \right)\] and simulating both steady states, in parallel. How derivatives are computed is configured on the runner: derivatives="finite_difference" always uses finite differences, displacement sets the relative change \(\Delta\) (default 1e-3, i.e. 0.1 %).

docs.title: Metaprogramming
Metaprogramming¶
docs.text:
mxlpy can inspect the Python source of your model functions and transform them into other representations — whether that is runnable code in another language, a symbolic LaTeX description, or a diff between two model variants.

This works for any model whose rate and derived functions are pure Python (no numpy, no closures over mutable state). The source is parsed with Python's ast module and then re-emitted in the target language.

Use cases include:

  • Sharing a model with collaborators who work in Rust, Julia, or TypeScript
  • Generating a LaTeX methods section directly from code
  • Tracking what changed between two model versions

docs.title: Code generation¶
docs.text: generate_mxlpy_code round-trips your model back into mxlpy builder syntax. This is useful for serialising a model that was constructed programmatically (e.g. after fitting or after reading from SBML) into a standalone Python file that can be shared or version-controlled without any runtime dependencies on the original construction logic.

docs.title: Free parameters¶
docs.text: By default, all parameters are baked into the generated function as constants. If you want to leave some parameters as inputs — for example to drive a parameter scan or a fitting loop in the target environment — pass their names as free_parameters. They will appear as additional function arguments instead of inlined literals.

docs.title: Derived quantities and initial conditions¶
docs.text:
Beyond the ODE function itself, a complete simulation needs two more pieces: a function that computes derived quantities from the current state (observables, intermediate fluxes), and the initial values for all variables.

The codegen object exposes these as .derived and .inits respectively. Both are emitted in the same target language as .model, so they can be dropped directly into the same file.

docs.title: Pruning derived quantities¶
docs.text: By default, the generated .derived function computes every derived quantity in the model. If you only need a subset — for example, you want to export a stripped-down function that outputs a single flux for a downstream optimiser — pass derived_to_calculate with the names you actually need. Quantities not in the list are omitted from the output function, and any intermediate computations required only by those omitted quantities are pruned automatically.

docs.title: LaTeX export¶
docs.text:
generate_model_code_latex produces a structured LaTeX representation of your model — parameters, variables, rate equations, and stoichiometry — formatted as tables ready to paste into a manuscript or supplementary material.

Two optional arguments let you customise the output:

  • gls — a dict mapping Python names to LaTeX names (e.g. {"k_in": r"\k_{in}"). Names without an entry are used verbatim.
  • long_name_cutoff — names longer than this threshold are automatically abbreviated to avoid overflowing table columns.

Call .as_tables() on the result to get the individual LaTeX table strings.

docs.title: Exporting diffs¶
docs.text:
When you modify a model — changing a parameter value, swapping a rate law, adding a species — generate_latex_diff highlights exactly what changed between two model versions as a LaTeX table. Unchanged rows are shown in normal weight; added or modified rows are highlighted.

Pass only_changes=True to suppress unchanged rows entirely (useful when models are large and only a handful of values differ). With only_changes=False (shown below) every row is included, giving the full context alongside the highlighted changes.

docs.title: Exporting a document¶
docs.text: generate_latex_document wraps any codegen result — either a single model or a diff — in a complete, compilable LaTeX document with the necessary preamble and package imports. This lets you go from a Model object to a .tex file you can compile directly with pdflatex, with no manual formatting needed.

docs.title: Placeholders / error handling¶
docs.text: If a model function uses constructs that mxlpy cannot translate - such as numpy calls, comprehensions, or external library calls - the LaTeX exporter inserts a red warning placeholder in place of that equation. The rest of the export is unaffected, so you still get a usable document for the parseable parts of your model.

docs.title: Model selection¶
docs.text:
Which of several candidate model structures does the data support? Adding reactions or regulations always improves the fit, so a more complex model has to improve it by enough to justify its extra parameters. mxlpy.select fits each candidate from several starting points and compares them with information criteria or likelihood-ratio tests:

  • AIC \(= 2k - 2\,\mathrm{LL}\), AICc \(= \mathrm{AIC} + \frac{2k(k+1)}{n-k-1}\) (small-sample correction), BIC \(= k \ln n - 2\,\mathrm{LL}\)

with \(k\) estimated parameters, \(n\) data points and the maximised log-likelihood \(\mathrm{LL}\). This needs a likelihood loss, fit.GaussianNll(sigma) for Gaussian measurement noise.

docs.title: Model space¶
docs.text:
A ModelSpace is a base model and named switches. Each combination of switches that are on is a candidate.

  • select.free_parameter(name, fixed_value) estimates a parameter when on and fixes it when off. Fixing it at the value where the feature vanishes (here a rate of 0) makes the models nested.
  • A plain function changes the model when the switch is on, e.g. adding a reaction.
  • select.Switch(on=..., off=..., fix_on=..., fix_off=...) covers the general case, and allowed= excludes combinations.

docs.title: Structure search¶
docs.text:
select.run searches the space. The parameters to estimate come with the distribution random starts are drawn from; each candidate estimates those its model has and doesn't fix.

  • forward turns one switch on at a time, backward one off.
  • adaptive alternates forward, backward and swap moves until none improves the criterion.
  • brute_force fits every candidate.

Every candidate is fitted from n_starts random starts plus a warm start from the optimum of the model the search came from.

docs.title: Likelihood-ratio tests¶
docs.text: For nested models, a likelihood-ratio test asks if the larger model fits significantly better. Here, the extra degradation of \(x\) doesn't improve the fit significantly, while the degradation of \(y\) does.

docs.title: Comparing explicit variants¶
docs.text: select.compare fits and ranks models given directly, e.g. alternative rate laws written by hand. The criteria are also available as plain functions (select.aic, select.aicc, select.bic, select.model_weights, select.lrt).

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from mxlpy.types import Array


@dataclass
class MyOwnDistribution:
    loc: float = 0.0
    scale: float = 1.0

    def sample(
        self,
        num: int,
        rng: np.random.Generator | None = None,
    ) -> Array:
        if rng is None:
            rng = np.random.default_rng()
        return rng.normal(loc=self.loc, scale=self.scale, size=num)

docs.title: Monte Carlo methods¶
docs.text:
Almost every parameter in biology is better described with a distribution than a single value. Monte-carlo methods allow you to capture the range of possible behaviour your model can exhibit. This is especially useful when you want to understand the uncertainty in your model's predictions.

mxlpy offers these Monte Carlo methods for all scans ...

+ =

and even for metabolic control analysis

+ =

In this tutorial we will mostly use the mxlpy.distributions and mxlpy.mca modules, which contain the functionality to sample from distributions and run distributed analyses.

docs.title: Sample values¶
docs.text:
To do any Monte-Carlo analysis, we first need to be able to sample values.

For that, you can use the sample function and distributions supplied by mxlpy. These are mostly thin wrappers around the numpy and scipy sampling methods.

docs.title: Steady-state¶
docs.text:
Using mc.steady_state you can calculate the steady-state distribution given the monte-carlo parameters.

This works analogously to the scan.steady_state function, except the index of the dataframes is always just an integer.

The parameters used can be obtained by result.parameters.

We will use a linear chain of reactions with two circles as an example model for this notebook.

\[ \begin{array}{c|c} \mathrm{Reaction} & \mathrm{Stoichiometry} \\ \hline v_0 & \varnothing \rightarrow{} \mathrm{x_1} \\ v_1 & -\mathrm{x_1} \rightarrow{} \mathrm{x_2} \\ v_2 & -\mathrm{x_1} \rightarrow{} \mathrm{x_3} \\ v_3 & -\mathrm{x_1} \rightarrow{} \mathrm{x_4} \\ v_4 & -\mathrm{x_4} \rightarrow{} \varnothing\\ v_5 & -\mathrm{x_2} \rightarrow{} \mathrm{x_1} \\ v_6 & -\mathrm{x_3} \rightarrow{} \mathrm{x_1} \\ \end{array} \]

docs.title: Time course¶
docs.text:
Using mc.time_course you can calculate time courses for sampled parameters.

+ =

This function works analogously to scan.time_course.

The pandas.DataFrames for concentrations and fluxes have a n x time pandas.MultiIndex.

The corresponding parameters can be found in result.parameters

docs.title: Protocol time course¶
docs.text:
Using mc.time_course_over_protocol you can calculate time courses for sampled parameters given a discrete protocol.

+ =

The pandas.DataFrames for concentrations and fluxes have a n x time pandas.MultiIndex. The corresponding parameters can be found in scan.parameters

docs.title: Metabolic control analysis¶
docs.text: mxlpy further has routines for monte-carlo distributed metabolic control analysis. This allows quantifying, whether the coefficients obtained from the MCA analysis are robust against parameter changes or whether they are just an artifact of a particular choice of parameters.

docs.text: Vary both monte carlo parameters as well as systematically scan for other parameters

docs.title: Custom distributions¶
docs.text:
If you want to create custom distributions, all you need to do is to create a class that follows the Distribution protocol, e.g. implements a sample function.

For API consistency, the sample method has to take rng argument, which can be ignored if not applicable.

def get_closed_cycle() -> tuple[Model, dict[str, int], dict[str, list[int]]]:
    """

    | Reaction       | Labelmap |
    | -------------- | -------- |
    | x1 ->[v1] x2   | [0, 1]   |
    | x2 ->[v2a] x3  | [0, 1]   |
    | x2 ->[v2b] x3  | [1, 0]   |
    | x3 ->[v3] x1   | [0, 1]   |

    """
    model = (
        Model()
        .add_parameters(
            {
                "vmax_1": 1.0,
                "km_1": 0.5,
                "vmax_2a": 1.0,
                "vmax_2b": 1.0,
                "km_2": 0.5,
                "vmax_3": 1.0,
                "km_3": 0.5,
            }
        )
        .add_variables({"x1": 1.0, "x2": 0.0, "x3": 0.0})
        .add_reaction(
            "v1",
            michaelis_menten_1s,
            stoichiometry={"x1": -1, "x2": 1},
            args=["x1", "vmax_1", "km_1"],
        )
        .add_reaction(
            "v2a",
            michaelis_menten_1s,
            stoichiometry={"x2": -1, "x3": 1},
            args=["x2", "vmax_2a", "km_2"],
        )
        .add_reaction(
            "v2b",
            michaelis_menten_1s,
            stoichiometry={"x2": -1, "x3": 1},
            args=["x2", "vmax_2b", "km_2"],
        )
        .add_reaction(
            "v3",
            michaelis_menten_1s,
            stoichiometry={"x3": -1, "x1": 1},
            args=["x3", "vmax_3", "km_3"],
        )
    )
    label_variables: dict[str, int] = {"x1": 2, "x2": 2, "x3": 2}
    label_maps: dict[str, list[int]] = {
        "v1": [0, 1],
        "v2a": [0, 1],
        "v2b": [1, 0],
        "v3": [0, 1],
    }
    return model, label_variables, label_maps

def _worker(
    x: tuple[tuple[int, pd.Series], tuple[int, pd.Series]],
    mapper: LinearLabelMapper,
    time: float,
    initial_labels: dict[str, int | list[int]],
) -> pd.Series:
    (_, y_ss), (_, v_ss) = x
    return (
        Simulator(mapper.build_model(y_ss, v_ss, initial_labels=initial_labels))
        .simulate(time)
        .get_result()
        .unwrap_or_err()
    ).variables.iloc[-1]


def get_label_distribution_at_time(
    model: Model,
    label_variables: dict[str, int],
    label_maps: dict[str, list[int]],
    time: float,
    initial_labels: dict[str, int | list[int]],
    ss_concs: pd.DataFrame,
    ss_fluxes: pd.DataFrame,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    mapper = LinearLabelMapper(
        model,
        label_variables=label_variables,
        label_maps=label_maps,
    )

    return pd.DataFrame(
        dict(
            parallelise(
                partial(
                    _worker, mapper=mapper, time=time, initial_labels=initial_labels
                ),
                inputs=list(
                    enumerate(
                        zip(
                            ss_concs.iterrows(),
                            ss_fluxes.iterrows(),
                            strict=True,
                        )
                    )
                ),  # type: ignore
                cache=None,
            )
        ),
        dtype=float,
    ).T


def inverse_parameter_elasticity(
    estimator: EstimatorProtocol,
    datum: pd.Series,
    *,
    normalized: bool = True,
    displacement: float = 1e-4,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    ref = estimator.predict(datum).iloc[0, :]

    coefs = {}
    for name, value in datum.items():
        up = coefs[name] = estimator.predict(
            pd.Series(datum.to_dict() | {name: value * 1 + displacement})
        ).iloc[0, :]
        down = coefs[name] = estimator.predict(
            pd.Series(datum.to_dict() | {name: value * 1 - displacement})
        ).iloc[0, :]
        coefs[name] = (up - down) / (2 * displacement * value)

    coefs = pd.DataFrame(coefs)
    if normalized:
        coefs *= datum / ref.to_numpy()

    return coefs

docs.title: Neural posterior estimation¶
docs.text:
Neural posterior estimation answers the question: what parameters could have generated the data I measured? Here you use an ODE model and prior knowledge about the parameters of interest to create synthetic data. You then use the generated synthetic data as the features and the input parameters as the targets to train an inverse problem. Once that training is successful, the neural network can now predict the input parameters for real world data.

You can use this technique for both steady-state as well as time course data. The only difference is in using scan.time_course.

Take care here to save the targets as well in case you use cached data :)

docs.title: Train NPE¶
docs.text: You can then train your neural posterior estimator using npe.train_torch_ss_estimator (or npe.train_torch_time_course_estimator if you have time course data).

docs.title: Sanity check: do prior and posterior match?¶
Re-entrant training¶
docs.text: As with the surrogates you often you don't know the amount of epochs you are going to need in order to reach the required loss. For the neural posterior estimation you can use the npe.TorchSteadyStateTrainer and npe.TorchTimeCourseTrainer respectively to continue training.

docs.title: Custom loss function¶
docs.text: You can use a custom loss function by simply injecting a function that takes the predicted tensor x and the data y and produces another tensor.
