Next we extend that idea to create a reaction. The only thing we need to change here is to also add the stoichiometries of the respective output variable.

I've renamed the output to v1 here to fit convention, but that is not technically necessary. mxlpy will always infer structurally into what kind of value your surrogate will be translated.

In [3]: Copied! 
m = Model()
m.add_variable("x", 1.0)
m.add_surrogate(
    "surrogate",
    surrogates.poly.Surrogate(
        model=Polynomial(coef=[2]),
        args=["x"],
        outputs=["v1"],
        stoichiometries={"v1": {"x": -1}},
    ),
)
m.add_derived("z", fns.add, args=["x", "v1"])

# Check output
m.get_right_hand_side()
m = Model() m.add_variable("x", 1.0) m.add_surrogate( "surrogate", surrogates.poly.Surrogate( model=Polynomial(coef=[2]), args=["x"], outputs=["v1"], stoichiometries={"v1": {"x": -1}}, ), ) m.add_derived("z", fns.add, args=["x", "v1"]) # Check output m.get_right_hand_side() Out[3]: 
x   -2.0
dtype: float64

Note that if you have multiple outputs, it is perfectly fine for them to mix between derived values and reactions.

Surrogate(
    model=...,
    args=["x", "y"],
    outputs=["d1", "v1"],               # outputs derived value d1 and rate v1
    stoichiometries={"v1": {"x": -1}},  # only rate v1 is given stoichiometries
)

We will start with a simple linear chain model

\[ \Large \varnothing \xrightarrow{v_1} x \xrightarrow{v_2} y \xrightarrow{v_3} \varnothing \]

where we want to read out the steady-state rate of \(v_3\) dependent on the fixed concentration of \(x\), while ignoring the inner state of the model.

\[ \Large x \xrightarrow{} ... \xrightarrow{v_3}\]

Since we need to fix a variable as an parameter, we can use the make_variable_static method to do that.

In [4]: Copied!

get_linear_chain_2v().make_variable_static("x").parameters
# Now "x" is a parameter get_linear_chain_2v().make_variable_static("x").parameters Out[4]: value unit k1 1 k2 2 k_out 1 x 1

And we can already create a function to create a model, which will take our surrogate as an input.

In [5]: Copied! 
def get_model_with_surrogate(surrogate: SurrogateProtocol) -> Model:
    model = Model()
    model.add_variables({"x": 1.0, "z": 0.0})

    # Adding the surrogate
    model.add_surrogate(
        "surrogate",
        surrogate,
        args=["x"],
        outputs=["v2"],
        stoichiometries={
            "v2": {"x": -1, "z": 1},
        },
    )

    # Note that besides the surrogate we haven't defined any other reaction!
    # We could have though
    return model

docs.title: Mechanistic Learning¶
docs.text:
Mechanistic learning is the intersection of mechanistic modelling and machine learning. mxlpy currently supports two such approaches: surrogates and neural posterior estimation.

In the following we will mostly use the mxlpy.surrogates and mxlpy.npe modules to learn about both approaches.

docs.title: Surrogate models¶
docs.text:
Surrogate models replace whole parts of a mechanistic model (or even the entire model) with machine learning models.

This allows combining together multiple models of arbitrary size, without having to worry about the internal state of each model. They are especially useful for improving the description of boundary effects, e.g. a dynamic description of downstream consumption.

docs.title: Manual construction¶
docs.text:
Surrogates can have return two kind of values in mxply: derived quantities and reactions.

We will start by defining a polynomial surrogate that will get the value of a variable x and output the derived quantity y. Note that due to their nature surrogates can take multiple inputs and return multiple outputs, so we will always use iterables when defining them.

We then also add a derived value z that uses the output of our surrogate to see that we are getting the correct output.

docs.title: Training a surrogate from data and using it¶
Create data¶
docs.text:
The surrogates used in the following will all use the steady-state fluxes depending on the inputs.

We can thus create the necessary training data usign scan.steady_state. Since this is usually a large amount of data, we recommend caching the results using Cache.

docs.title: Polynomial surrogate¶
docs.text:
We can train our polynomial surrogate using train_polynomial_surrogate. By default this will train polynomials for the degrees (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7), but you can change that by using the degrees argument. The function returns the trained surrogate and the training information for the different polynomial degrees.

Currently the polynomial surrogates are limited to a single feature and a single target

docs.title: Neural network surrogate using PyTorch¶
docs.text:
Neural networks are designed to capture highly complex and nonlinear relationships. Through layers of neurons and activation functions, neural networks can learn intricate patterns that are not easily represented by e.g. a polynomial. They have the flexibility to approximate any continuous function, given sufficient depth and appropriate training.

You can train a neural network surrogate based on the popular PyTorch library using train_torch_surrogate. That function takes the features, targets and the number of epochs as inputs for it's training.

train_torch_surrogate returns the trained surrogate, as well as the training loss. It is always a good idea to check whether that training loss approaches 0.

docs.title: Re-entrant training¶
docs.text: Quite often you don't know the amount of epochs you are going to need in order to reach the required loss. In this case, you can directly use the TorchSurrogateTrainer class to continue training.

docs.title: Troubleshooting¶
docs.text: It often can make sense to check specific predictions of the surrogate. For example, what does it predict when the inputs are all 0?

docs.title: Using keras instead of torch¶
docs.text: If you installed keras, you can use it with exactly the same interface torch

docs.title: Saving and loading surrogates¶
docs.text:
Training can be expensive, so a trained surrogate can be saved with surrogate.save(path) and restored with surrogates.load(path). Persistence is delegated to the backend's own format. path is a directory holding surrogate.json (args, outputs, stoichiometries, units / targets) next to the model file:

backend model file needs model= on load torch model.pt (state_dict) yes equinox model.eqx (eqx.tree_serialise_leaves) yes keras model.keras no poly model.json no qss model.dill no

torch and equinox only store the weights, so loading needs a freshly built network with the same architecture (model=), into which the weights are loaded. A small function building your architecture makes that easy, and it also works for networks that mxlpy.save can't export (e.g. LSTMs or custom modules).

docs.title: Custom loss function¶
docs.text: You can use a custom loss function by simply injecting a function that takes the predicted tensor x and the data y and produces another tensor.

The pure neural ODE settles into a poor solution: it follows the first few time points, then drifts off monotonically instead of oscillating. Without a prior, it has to discover the oscillation from data alone, and here it doesn't within the training budget.

Part of the difficulty is structural. A Node is an autonomous ODE on the two observed variables, so exactly one trajectory passes through each point of the (prey, predator) plane, and trajectories can never cross. Dynamics close to that limit need a very contorted vector field, which is hard to learn, and dynamics beyond it, such as time-dependent forcing that makes the data revisit a state with a different velocity, can't be represented at all.

docs.title: Universal Differential Equations¶
docs.text:
A Universal Differential Equation (UDE) combines a mechanistic ODE with a neural network to learn unknown or partially-known dynamics from data. The ODE encodes prior biological knowledge; the neural network (called the NDE component) learns residual dynamics the ODE cannot explain on its own.

This notebook demonstrates UDE training on a Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system with an unknown external forcing term.

docs.title: Baseline: mechanistic ODE¶
docs.text: The Lotka-Volterra system describes predator-prey dynamics with four parameters (a, b, c, d). This serves as the mechanistic prior — the part of the system we already understand and can encode explicitly.

docs.title: Training the UDE¶
docs.text:
We construct a Ude by combining the mechanistic Ode with a small neural network (Node). The op="+" means the NDE output is added to the ODE right-hand side at each time step.

Training uses train, which freezes the ODE parameters and only optimises the neural network weights. A curriculum schedule gradually increases the proportion of the trajectory used for loss computation, which helps avoid poor local minima early in training.

docs.title: Separate the contribution of each model part¶
docs.text: After training we can evaluate the ODE and NDE components independently along the predicted trajectory. jax.vmap maps each component over all time points in one call. This decomposition reveals what the neural network actually learned — ideally it should recover the unknown forcing signal.

docs.title: Neural ODEs without a prior: Node¶
docs.text:
Node is the neural component on its own, without any mechanistic prior:

\[\frac{dy}{dt} = s \cdot \text{MLP}(y, \text{args})\]

where \(s\) is out_scale. We train it on the same data, with the same budget and solver settings as the UDE above. To compare the models fairly, the remaining sections share one helper.

docs.title: Augmented neural ODEs: Anode¶
docs.text:
Augmented neural ODEs (Dupont et al., 2019) lift this restriction by integrating in a larger space. The state \(y\) (n_obs dimensions) is extended by n_hidden hidden dimensions \(h\). The ODE runs on the latent state \(z = (y, h)\), and trajectories that cross in observation space can be separated along \(h\).

A latent mapper encodes the initial observation into \(z_0\) and decodes the latent trajectory back to observations. integrate and simulate_* always take and return observations; the latent state stays internal.

Mapper Encode \(y_0 \to z_0\) Decode \(z \to y\) SoftLatentMapper \((y_0, \text{linear}(y_0))\) \(\text{linear}(z)\) HardLatentMapper \((y_0, \text{linear}(y_0))\) \(z_{[:n_{obs}]}\) FullLatentMapper \(\text{linear}(y_0)\) \(\text{linear}(z)\) MixedLatentMapper \((y_0, \text{linear}(y_0))\) \((1-\alpha)\,z_{[:n_{obs}]} + \alpha\,\text{linear}(z)\) TrainableZ0LatentMapper \((y_0, z_0^{\text{learned}})\) as MixedLatentMapper

Anode defaults to SoftLatentMapper. The two annealed mappers need alpha, which you pass through integrate*(alpha=...) or IntegrationSettings(alpha=...). Lowering alpha over a training curriculum moves the decode from the learned map towards the plain slice.

docs.title: Augmented UDEs: AugUde¶
docs.text:
AugUde combines a mechanistic Ode with an Anode, in the same way that Ude combines it with a Node. With \(d = \text{Anode}(t, z, \text{args})\) on the latent state \(z = (y, h)\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{dy}{dt} &= \text{op}\big(\text{ODE}(t, y, \text{args}),\ d_{[:n_{obs}]}\big) \\ \frac{dh}{dt} &= d_{[n_{obs}:]} \end{aligned} \]

The mechanistic model only sees the observed slice \(y = z_{[:n_{obs}]}\), so the hidden dimensions reach the observed dynamics only through the neural correction. This follows the hybrid-modelling literature. Augmented NODEs define the hidden dimensions for the neural model. Physics-plus-correction hybrids such as APHYNITY (Yin et al., 2021) keep the mechanistic term on the physical state. In latent hybridisation (Qian et al., 2021), the expert ODE runs on its own variables and drives the ML variables, not the other way round. If unobserved variables have known mechanisms, add them to the Ode itself rather than as hidden dimensions.

Because the mechanistic part reads \(z_{[:n_{obs}]}\), the latent mapper has to keep the observation there:

  • HardLatentMapper is the interpretable choice: the decoded observations are exactly the state the mechanistic model sees.
  • MixedLatentMapper and TrainableZ0LatentMapper anneal towards it.
  • SoftLatentMapper is allowed, but its learned decode means the reported observations differ from what the ODE acts on.
  • FullLatentMapper doesn't keep the observation and is rejected.

docs.title: Flux-based variants¶
docs.text:
Every model above has a flux-based counterpart for models built with reactions and stoichiometry. They combine the mechanistic and neural fluxes, then map them through the mechanistic stoichiometry nv:

State-based Flux-based Neural part Ode FluxOde none Node FluxNode flux MLP Ude FluxUde FluxNode Anode FluxAnode flux + Markov MLP AugUde FluxAugUde FluxAnode

In FluxAnode and FluxAugUde the hidden dimensions can't go through nv, which only maps onto the observed variables. Their dynamics come from a separate Markov MLP:

\[ \begin{aligned} v &= \text{op}\big(\text{fluxes}_{\text{ODE}}(t, y, \text{args}),\ \text{fluxes}_{\text{NN}}(t, z, \text{args})\big) \\ \frac{dy}{dt} &= N v \\ \frac{dh}{dt} &= \text{Markov}(z, \text{args}) \end{aligned} \]

FluxNode.from_flux_ode and FluxAnode.from_flux_ode build the neural part with the mechanistic model's variable names, flux names, stoichiometry and readouts. Simulations of FluxUde/FluxAugUde report the combined fluxes, and additionally the ode_fluxes and nn_fluxes that went into them. The model below is untrained; it only shows the construction.

def logistic_harvest(x: float, r: float, capacity: float, h: float) -> float:
    return r * x * (1 - x / capacity) - h * x


def fraction(x: float, capacity: float) -> float:
    return x / capacity


def get_model() -> OdeModelBuilder:
    return (
        OdeModelBuilder()
        .add_parameters({"r": 1.0, "capacity": 10.0, "h": 0.2})
        .add_diff_eq(
            "x",
            fn=logistic_harvest,
            args=["x", "r", "capacity", "h"],
            initial_value=0.5,
        )
        .add_derived("saturation", fn=fraction, args=["x", "capacity"])
    )


model = get_model()
model.diff_eqs

import { OdeModelBuilder } from "@computational-biology-aachen/mxlweb-core";
import { Add, Divide, Minus, Mul, Name, Num } from "@computational-biology-aachen/mxlweb-core/mathml";

export function initModel(): OdeModelBuilder {
    return new OdeModelBuilder()
      .addParameter("r", {
        value: 1.0,
        texName: 'r',
      })
      .addParameter("capacity", {
        value: 10.0,
        texName: 'capacity',
      })
      .addParameter("h", {
        value: 0.2,
        texName: 'h',
      })
      .addVariable("x", {
        value: 0.5,
        texName: 'x',
      })
      .addAssignment("saturation", {
        fn: new Divide([new Name("x"), new Name("capacity")]),
        texName: 'saturation',
      })
      .setDifferential("x", new Add([new Minus([new Mul([new Name("h"), new Name("x")])]), new Mul([new Name("r"), new Name("x"), new Add([new Num(1.0), new Minus([new Divide([new Name("x"), new Name("capacity")])])])])]))
  }

docs.title: ODE models¶
docs.text:
mxlpy has three model builders, which differ in how the right hand side of the system is written down:

Builder Right hand side Typical use KineticModelBuilder (Model) \(N \cdot v(x)\): reactions with rate laws and a stoichiometric matrix metabolic & signalling networks OdeModelBuilder \(\frac{dx}{dt} = f(x)\): one differential equation per variable phenomenological models, equations taken from a paper SteadyStateModelBuilder no variables, only explicit functions of parameters algebraic / steady-state models, see Steady-state models

This notebook covers the OdeModelBuilder. Use it when your model is naturally written as differential equations rather than as a reaction network. Since there are no reactions, an OdeModelBuilder has no fluxes and no stoichiometries.

As an example we use logistic growth with a constant harvesting rate \(h\)

\[\frac{dx}{dt} = r x \left(1 - \frac{x}{K}\right) - h x\]

which has the non-trivial steady state \(x^* = K \left(1 - \frac{h}{r}\right)\).

docs.title: Building the model¶
docs.text:
Instead of add_reaction, every variable gets exactly one differential equation via add_diff_eq, which also sets the variable's initial value. Parameters and derived quantities work just like in the KineticModelBuilder.

As with all builders, use named functions instead of lambdas (they need to be inspectable and pickle-able).

docs.title: Simulation¶
docs.text:
An OdeModelBuilder is simulated with the same Simulator as a KineticModelBuilder. The result is an OdeSimulation, which offers the same access patterns as a Simulation, minus everything flux related.

Routines like scans and fits configure the simulation with an OdeRunner instead, see the integrator configuration.

docs.title: Parameter scans¶
docs.text: All functions of the scan module accept an OdeModelBuilder. Their results have the same shape as for a KineticModelBuilder, just without fluxes. The same goes for the Monte Carlo routines in mc.

docs.title: Fitting¶
docs.text:
All fitting routines except the reaction carousel accept an OdeModelBuilder. The returned Fit contains a copy of the OdeModelBuilder.

Here we create some synthetic data with known parameters and fit the model to it.

docs.title: Response coefficients¶
docs.text: Response coefficients describe how much the steady state changes if a parameter is perturbed. For an OdeModelBuilder they are available for the variables. With the default normalisation, the steady state \(x^* = K (1 - h / r)\) responds proportionally to the carrying capacity \(K\).

docs.title: Export¶
docs.text: OdeModelBuilder models can be saved to the native .mxl.json format with mxlpy.save / mxlpy.load, and exported to MxlWeb, which natively supports differential equation models.

docs.title: Current limitations¶
docs.text:
Everything about reactions, fluxes or stoichiometries only applies to the KineticModelBuilder. Not supported for the OdeModelBuilder are thus

  • flux elasticities and rate characteristics in mca, reaction carousels, model comparisons and label models
  • Jacobians (Simulator(..., use_jacobian=True) falls back to finite differences with a warning) and events

docs.title: Parallelization¶
docs.text:
mxlpy allows easy parallelisation of functions using the parallel module.

The API of this is built in a way to allow for easy mapping, saving results and stopping execution of long running functions.

Sharp edge: be aware that the usual issues of multiprocessing on Windows apply

docs.title: Basic API¶
docs.text:
The most basic call to parallelise just requires

  1. A function that consumes an input and returns it's result
  2. A tuple of (key, input)

docs.title: Restricting cores¶
docs.text: By default parallelise will use all available CPU cores. In case you want to limit that, you can use the max_workers parameter to set an explicit number.

docs.title: Caching results¶
docs.text:
By supplying the Cache class, you can automatically save and retrieve your calculated values.

The default settings are

  • Write results into .cache folder
  • Write and load a pickle file, using {key}.p of inputs as the name

docs.title: Timeouts¶
docs.text:
You can set a timeout for long-running functions. This timeout runs per function call, so you can recover all other runs without any problems.

E.g. check below how a is retrieved, while b caused a timeout and is thus missing.

docs.title: Progress bar customisation¶
docs.text:
We use tqdm as our progress bar.

You can disable it using the disable_tqdm flag

docs.title: Running sequentially¶
docs.text:
You can run a function sequentially using parallel=False. While it might seems odd in the beginning to do this, the point is easy refactoring in cases where you might nest analyses.

You generally don't want n processes to spawn n new processes each. The parallel=False flag allows you to re-use analyses written using parallel=True with only a single change.

This can also occasionally be useful for de-bugging functions running in parallel

docs.title: Numerical parameter identifiability¶
docs.text: See the course by Marisa Eisenberg for an excellent introduction into the topic

docs.title: Profile likelihood¶
docs.text:
The profile likelihood of a parameter fixes it at values stepping away from the optimum and refits all other parameters at each of them. The increase of the objective along the profile shows how well the data determines the parameter:

  • with a likelihood loss like fit.GaussianNll(sigma), the likelihood-ratio test bounds the alpha confidence interval where the objective has increased by chi2.ppf(alpha, 1) / 2
  • a profile that crosses this threshold on both sides is identifiable
  • one that reaches the end of the profiled range on a side without crossing it is practically non-identifiable, the data only bounds it on one side, if at all
  • a flat profile is structurally non-identifiable, other parameters fully compensate for it

Steps adapt to the profile, dense near the optimum and sparse where it is flat, and both sides of all parameters are profiled in parallel. With transform="log" parameters are profiled in log10 steps, which suits values spanning orders of magnitude. For losses that aren't likelihoods, pass the threshold yourself.

We add measurement noise to the data, fit the model and profile both parameters from the optimum.

docs.title: Fisher information¶
docs.text:
Profile likelihoods need many fits per parameter. A much cheaper first look is the Fisher information at the optimum, which needs a single sensitivity evaluation. From the noise-weighted sensitivities of the residuals S it computes F = SᵀS, whose inverse is the asymptotic covariance of the parameters. It assumes Gaussian noise and a model that is approximately linear around the optimum.

Pass the noise level as sigma (a scalar, one value per observable or per data point). Without it, the noise variance is estimated from the residuals.

docs.title: Fast identifiability test¶
docs.text:
Profiles need many fits per parameter, the Fisher information assumes the model is approximately linear around the optimum. identify.identifiability_test is a cheap numerical check in between: it refits the parameters from n_fits random points around the optimum, with a penalty that pulls them to distance radius from it (in log10 units with transform="log", the default, so radius=1 is a decade).

  • if a pulled fit reaches the radius without increasing the objective by more than the threshold (chi2.ppf(0.95, 1) / 2 for likelihood losses, else threshold_rtol times the objective), the objective is flat in that direction
  • fits that stop short of the radius without exceeding the threshold (usually because of bounds) make the result inconclusive, which the test warns about
  • the parameters that moved along it (by at least min_displacement · radius) are non-identifiable

This costs a handful of fits regardless of the number of parameters, which makes it a good routine check after every fit. It is a check, not a proof: flat directions the random starts miss go unnoticed, so follow up with profiles of the flagged parameters.

Both SIR parameters pass the test.

docs.title: Related parameters¶
docs.text: Along the profile of a non-identifiable parameter, other parameters compensate for it so the fit stays the same. identify.related_parameters regresses each such profile on the paths of the other parameters and returns the combination that stays constant, which is what the data actually determine. With log parameters, log10(beta) + log10(c) ≈ const means that the product beta · c is identifiable.

docs.title: Model parameterisation¶
docs.text:
Obtaining experimentally measured parameters can be challenging.

Using the Brenda enzymes database we can obtain distributions of enzymatic parameters for a wide range of organisms.

We can do that with the mxlpy.parameterise module.

These distributions can then in turn be used with our Monte-Carlo methods to capture the range of possible behaviour your model can exhibit.

+ =

In order to obtain the parameters for a given Enzyme commision number (ec) we will manually download the database. You have to do this manually due to the brenda licensing terms.

Note: we have created a small copy of just the rubisco data here to keep the documentation running. Adjust your brenda_path accordingly

docs.text:
In [1]: Copied! 
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from matplotlib.figure import Figure

from example_models import get_sir, get_sird
from mxlpy import Model, Simulator, plot, report


def plot_difference(r_old: pd.DataFrame, r_new: pd.DataFrame) -> Figure:
    rel_diff = (r_new - r_old) / r_old
    largest_diff = rel_diff.abs().mean().fillna(0).sort_values().tail(n=3)

    fig, ax = plot.one_axes()
    plot.lines(r_new, ax=ax)
    lines = dict(zip(r_new.columns, ax.lines, strict=True))
    for f, i in enumerate(reversed(largest_diff.index), start=2):
        line = lines[i]
        line.set_linewidth(line.get_linewidth() * f)

    plot.reset_prop_cycle(ax)
    plot.lines(r_old, ax=ax, alpha=0.25, legend=False)
    ax.set(xlabel="Time / a.u.", ylabel="Relative Population")
    return fig

You can further expand the report with user-defined analysis functions that are being run for both models. Here for example we perform a normal simulation and then plot the time course, highlighting the variables that changed the most.

All user-defined analysis functions have to take two models and the directory where plots are to be stored as an input and output a description in markdown as well as the path of the final image, so that it can be inserted into the report correctly.

def analyse_concentrations(m1: Model, m2: Model, img_dir: Path) -> tuple[str, Path]:
    r_old = Simulator(m1).simulate(100).get_result().unwrap_or_err()
    r_new = Simulator(m2).simulate(100).get_result().unwrap_or_err()
    fig = plot_difference(r_old.variables, r_new.variables)
    if not (path := img_dir / "concentration.png").exists():
        fig.savefig(path, dpi=300)
    plt.close(fig)
    return "## Comparison of largest changing", path

    get_sird(),
    analyses=[analyse_concentrations],
    m1_name="SIR",

)

docs.title: Reports¶
docs.text:
To make it easy to communicate changes between two models, mxlpy has conveniece functions in the report module. By default, the report.markdown function will take two models as inputs and then compare both the structure of the two models as well as numerical differences in dependent values as well as the right hand side.

The report is color-coded consistently, with green referring to new features, orange referring to updates / changes and red referring to deleted quantities.

def _pickle_name(k: Hashable) -> str:
    return f"{k}.p"


def _pickle_load(file: Path) -> Any:
    with file.open("rb") as fp:
        return pickle.load(fp)


def _pickle_save(file: Path, data: Any) -> None:
    with file.open("wb") as fp:
        pickle.dump(data, fp)


_ = Cache(

    load_fn=_pickle_load,

)

docs.title: Parameter scans¶
docs.text:
Parameter scans allow you to systematically assess the behaviour of your model dependent on the value of one or more parameters. mxlpy has routines to scan over, and easily visualise time courses, protocol time courses, and steady states for one or more parameters.

For this, we import the scan and plot modules from which contain the respective routines.

docs.title: Steady-state¶
docs.text:
The steady-state scan takes a pandas.DataFrame of parameters to be scanned as an input and returns the steady-states at the respective parameter values.

The DataFrame can take an arbitrary number of parameters and should be in the following format

n k1 0 1 1 1.2 2 1.4

As an example we will use a linear chain of two reactions like this

\[ \varnothing \xrightarrow{v_1} S \xrightarrow{v_2} P \xrightarrow{v_3} \varnothing\]

docs.title: Combinations¶
docs.text:
Often you want to scan over multiple parameters at the same time. The recommended way to do this is to use the cartesian_product function, which takes a parameter_name: values mapping and creates a pandas.DataFrame of their combinations from it (think nested for loop).

In the case the parameters DataFrame contains more than one column, the returned pandas.DataFrame will contain a pandas.MultiIndex.

docs.title: Time course¶
docs.text: You can perform a time course for each of the parameter values, resulting in a distribution of time courses. The index now also contains the time, so even for one parameter a pandas.MultiIndex is used.

docs.title: Protocol¶
docs.text: The same can be done for protocols.

docs.title: Parallel execution¶
docs.text:
By default, all scans are executed in parallel. To do this, they internally use the parallelise function defined by mxlpy.

Tip: You can also use this function for other analyses as it is not specific to any mxlpy constructs.

The parallelise takes a function of type T and an iterable of a key: T pair. The key is used to map the results to a given input and for caching (see below).

docs.title: Caching¶
docs.text:
In case the simulations take a significant amount of time to run, it makes sense to cache the results on disk. You can do that by adding a cache to the parallelise function (and thus to all scan functions as well).

parallelise(...,  cache=Cache())

The first time the scan is run, the calculations are done, every subsequent time the results are loaded.

Screen, then quantify. Morris is the cheap first pass that discards parameters you can safely fix; Sobol is the more expensive second pass that puts numbers on the ones that survive. Used together they turn a high-dimensional parameter space into a short, ranked list of the parameters worth fitting or measuring.

docs.title: Global sensitivity analysis¶
docs.text:
Before committing to an expensive analysis — parameter fitting, profile-likelihood identifiability, or a full variance-based Sobol decomposition — it pays to ask a cheaper question first: which parameters actually move the output at all?

The Morris method answers exactly that. It is an elementary-effects screening method: it perturbs one parameter at a time along a handful of random trajectories through parameter space and measures how much the output changes. With only n_trajectories * (k + 1) model evaluations (k = number of parameters) it sorts parameters into three buckets:

Reading Interpretation low mu_star unimportant — safe to fix to a constant high mu_star, low sigma important and roughly linear high mu_star, high sigma important and nonlinear or interacting

where mu_star is the mean absolute elementary effect and sigma its standard deviation across trajectories.

docs.title: The output function¶
docs.text:
Sensitivity is always measured with respect to some scalar output of the model. Rather than ship a fixed menu of reductions, sensitivity.morris asks you for an output function:

output(model, samples: pd.DataFrame) -> np.ndarray

It receives the model and the full matrix of parameter samples (one row per sample, one column per parameter) and returns one scalar per row. The natural way to write it is to lean on mxlpy.scan, which already evaluates the whole sample matrix in parallel, caches results, and — importantly — returns NaN for any sample whose integration failed. That NaN flows straight through to the sensitivity indices, so failed runs surface honestly instead of being silently masked.

Any reduction scan can express is available for free:

  • steady-state value of a species: scan.steady_state(model, to_scan=samples).variables[name]
  • peak value over a time course: scan.time_course(model, to_scan=samples, time_points=...).get_agg_per_run("max")[name]
  • area under the curve: pass np.trapezoid as the aggregator to get_agg_per_run

Here we screen the steady-state concentration of x in a simple linear chain \(\varnothing \xrightarrow{v_1} x \xrightarrow{v_2} y \xrightarrow{v_3} \varnothing\) against its three rate constants.

docs.title: Visualising the screen¶
docs.text: Two plots make the screen easy to read: a ranking of mu_star (with its confidence interval), and a mu_star-vs-sigma scatter that separates linear from nonlinear influence.

docs.title: Cost and reproducibility¶
docs.text:
Morris is cheap: with n_trajectories=20 and k=3 parameters the screen above used 20 * (3 + 1) = 80 model evaluations — a tiny fraction of what a variance-based method would need. That is the point: screen first with Morris, then quantify the survivors with a more expensive method.

Pass a seed for reproducible sampling and bootstrap confidence intervals, and tune num_levels (default 4) to control the granularity of the sampling grid.

docs.title: From screening to quantification: Sobol indices¶
docs.text:
Morris tells you which parameters matter; it does not tell you how much each one explains, nor cleanly separate a parameter's own effect from the effect of its interactions. The Sobol method does both. It is a variance-based method: it decomposes the total variance of the output into the share attributable to each parameter.

It returns two indices per parameter:

Index Meaning S1 (first-order) fraction of output variance explained by that parameter alone ST (total-order) fraction explained by that parameter including all of its interactions

The gap ST - S1 is the interaction signal: if it is large, the parameter matters mostly through other parameters rather than on its own.

sobol takes the same output and param_bounds contract as morris, so the reduction you already wrote carries over unchanged. The one new knob is n_samples (the Saltelli base sample size), which must be a power of two — passing anything else raises a ValueError. The total cost is n_samples * (k + 2) model evaluations, which is why you screen with Morris first and reserve Sobol for the survivors.

docs.title: Serialization
Native JSON serialization¶
docs.text:
MxlPy can read and write models in a native, version-controllable JSON format (.mxl.json). Unlike SBML, which is the standard for cross-tool interchange, the native format captures the full MxlPy model structure - variables, parameters, reactions, derived quantities and readouts - and is designed to produce clean, meaningful diffs in version control.

Rate expressions are stored as trees of math nodes using the node set shared with MxlWeb, so the same files can be consumed by both tools.

docs.title: Saving and loading¶
docs.text: mxlpy.save writes the model, mxlpy.load reconstructs it. A loaded model is behaviourally identical to the original and simulates to the same result.

docs.title: Lossless round-trip¶
docs.text: The format round-trips through SymPy, so the loaded model uses generated rate functions (not the original named ones) but produces identical dynamics. save -> load -> save also reaches a stable fixed point.

docs.title: Notes¶
docs.text:
• The file references a $schema from the shared mxl-schemas repository, giving editor validation and autocompletion for .mxl.json files.
  • Surrogates and rate functions that cannot be parsed into an expression raise mxlpy.types.SerializationError. Use SBML (mxlpy.sbml) for those, or for cross-tool interchange.
  • The spec_version field tracks the format version; it is shared with MxlWeb and decoupled from the MxlPy package version.

docs.title: Stability analysis¶
docs.text:
mxlpy offers routines to easily visualise the stability of the model over a wide range of parameters.

plot.trajectories2d shows the vector field depending on the values of two variables as a quiver plot.

docs.title: Steady-state models
Steady-state models¶
docs.text:
A SteadyStateModelBuilder describes a model without any dynamics: there are no variables, only parameters and quantities derived from them. This makes it a good fit for algebraic models, e.g. analytic steady-state solutions, response curves or allometric relationships.

Because there is nothing to integrate, a SteadyStateModelBuilder is never simulated. Instead it is evaluated directly, which is both simpler and much faster.

As an example we use an enzyme following Michaelis-Menten kinetics, which is competitively inhibited by \(I\)

\[ v = \frac{V_{\max} \cdot S}{K_m \left(1 + \frac{I}{K_i}\right) + S} \qquad V_{\max} = k_{cat} \cdot E_{tot}\]

docs.title: Building the model¶
docs.text: Parameters and derived quantities work just like in the other builders. Parameters can also be initial assignments, and derived quantities can depend on each other in any order.

docs.title: Evaluation¶
docs.text: evaluate returns all derived values as a pandas.Series. This replaces the Simulator for this builder.

docs.title: Parameter scans¶
docs.text:
scan.steady_state accepts a SteadyStateModelBuilder and evaluates it for every row of to_scan. It returns a SteadyStateScan holding one Evaluation per scanned value. Since there are no variables, the values are accessed via combined or get_args.

Nothing is integrated, so there is no integrator to configure and no y0. Time course and protocol scans are not available for this builder.

docs.title: Fitting¶
docs.text:
fit.steady_state accepts a SteadyStateModelBuilder and fits its parameters to a pandas.Series of data. The data can contain any parameter or derived value.

Here we assume we measured the rate \(v\) and the saturation of the enzyme at \(S = 2\) and fit \(K_m\) and \(k_{cat}\).

docs.title: Response coefficients¶
docs.text: Response coefficients describe how much the derived values change if a parameter is perturbed. As the model is evaluated instead of simulated, these are just the (normalised) derivatives of evaluate(). For example, the rate \(v\) responds proportionally to \(k_{cat}\).

docs.title: Export¶
docs.text: SteadyStateModelBuilder models can be saved to the native .mxl.json format with mxlpy.save / mxlpy.load, and exported to MxlWeb, which evaluates them in the browser.

docs.title: Current limitations¶
docs.text: The SteadyStateModelBuilder supports every routine whose question makes sense without dynamics: steady-state scans, fits (including group, ensemble and joint fits), Monte Carlo methods, response coefficients and sensitivity analysis. Time courses, protocols and everything about reactions or fluxes don't apply to it.

The best spline recovers the timing and size of the pulse from measurements of \(x\) alone.
 
Why did we fix \(k\)? A flexible input can absorb any degradation constant: for every \(k\), the input \(u(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} + k\,x\) reproduces the same \(x(t)\). So \(k\) and the input can't be estimated together from \(x\) alone, and fitting both would give an arbitrary \(k\) with a matching input. Inputs are identifiable only together with enough independent information about the rest of the model. For a confidence band of the estimated stimulus, profile the knot values with identify.profile_likelihood.
 
Other options of the spline:
 
     
  • monotone=True uses a monotone cubic, which doesn't overshoot between knots
    •  
  • initial_slope=0.0 fixes the slope at the first knot, e.g. for an input that starts at steady state
    •  
 
Splines are piecewise polynomials whose expression grows roughly quadratically with the number of knots, so up to about 20 knots are cheap.

docs.title: Time-dependent inputs¶
docs.text:
Models are often driven by an external signal: a ligand added to the medium, light, a drug dose, or an upstream species that isn't part of the model. mxlpy.fns_input provides parameterised shapes for such inputs. Their parameters are ordinary model parameters, so they can be fitted together with the kinetic ones. This lets you estimate an unknown input from downstream measurements ("input estimation").

Unlike protocols, which change parameters between integrations, inputs are model functions of time. They work with fitting, forward sensitivities, symbolic analysis, serialisation and code generation.

docs.title: Shapes¶
docs.text:
All inputs are used as derived values with "time" as the first argument.

  • smooth_step(t, level1, switch_time, level2, steepness): logistic switch
  • step(t, level1, switch_time, level2): hard switch. It is discontinuous, so prefer smooth_step, or a protocol if the levels aren't fitted
  • periodic_step(t, low, high, period, on_fraction, sharpness): smooth periodic switching, e.g. day and night
  • bolus(t, area, peak_time, width): Gaussian pulse with a given total area, e.g. an injected dose
  • multi_step(switch_times, steepness=...): factory for several switches at fixed times with fitted levels (steepness=None for hard switches)
  • cubic_spline(knots, positive=False, monotone=False, initial_slope=None): factory for a spline through fitted values at fixed knot times

docs.title: Estimating an unknown stimulus¶
docs.text:
As an example, a species \(x\) is produced in response to a stimulus \(u(t)\) and degraded with rate constant \(k\):

\[\frac{dx}{dt} = u(t) - k\,x\]

We only measure \(x\), and we know \(k\) from a separate experiment (e.g. the decay after washing the stimulus out). The stimulus, unknown to us, is a pulse on top of a baseline.

docs.title: How many knots?¶
docs.text: Too few knots can't follow the pulse, and too many fit the noise. We fit the knot values for several knot counts and compare the fits with select.compare, which ranks models by an information criterion (here BIC, see model selection).
